Past medical history includes a small subarachnoid haemorrhage four years ago and left adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma.

He takes doxazosin 4mg and simvastatin 40mg once daily. He has no allergies.

When asking about family history, he explains that he was adopted as a baby and so is unsure if there are any illnesses that run in the family.

What is the most likely diagnosis that would explain the above findings?
explanation:
Patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome may develop retinal haemangiomas which present as a vitreous haemorrhage

All of the above answers can be grouped into an 'umbrella term' of phakomatoses.

Neurofibromatosis type I (NF1) commonly causes the development of multiple neurofibromas of the skin and cafe au lait spots. NF1 commonly affects the eyes with the appearance of Lisch nodules and optic gliomas of the optic nerve. NF1 is not associated with phaeochromocytoma or vitreous haemorrhage.

Neurofibromatosis type II (NF2) causes schwannomas and meningiomas with people commonly suffering from sensorineural hearing loss secondary to acoustic neuromas. NF2 generally affects the nervous system and doesn't have eye involvement.

Sturge-Weber syndrome is a rare condition associated with developmental delay, port-wine stains, glaucoma and seizures. There is an increased risk in the development of retinoblastoma.

Tuberous sclerosis commonly causes angiofibromas and moles of the skin along with developmental delay. It commonly affects multiple systems of the body, in particular the nervous system with epilepsy and seizures. Eye signs include astrocytic hamartomas.

Von Hippel Lindau syndrome (VHL) is the correct answer. Patients develop multiple cysts and tumours affecting a large number of body systems. Subarachnoid haemorrhage is common secondary to cerebral haemangiomas and vitreous haemorrhage is a common presentation for retinal haemangiomas. Patients are also at increased risk of phaeochromocytoma, clear-cell renal cancer and cysts involving the pancreas, liver and epididymis.

question:
A 55-year-old man is referred to neurology outpatients with reports of a three-month history of weakness in his upper and lower limbs. He has no past medical history. He is right-handed.

On examination, there were fasciculations and muscle atrophy in the right upper limb. Power was 4/5 in the right upper limb and left lower limb. Hyperreflexia of the right biceps reflex was noted along with hyporeflexia of the bilateral knee reflexes. The plantar reflexes were upgoing. The sensation was normal throughout.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following treatments will confer a prognostic benefit?
explanation:
Motor neuron disease - riluzole

Riluzole is correct. The patient presents with insidious weakness and mixed upper (hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) and lower (fasciculations, atrophy, hyporeflexia) motor neuron signs. The most likely cause is motor neurone disease (MND). Given the presentation is limb predominant, this is likely to represent the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis variant of this disease. Riluzole retards the onset of ventilator-dependence in some patients and potentially may increase survival by two to three months.

Intravenous immunoglobulin is incorrect. This treatment may be indicated in conditions such as Guillain-Barre syndrome and inflammatory myopathies, which can present with weakness. However, these conditions are not associated with UMN signs and are therefore less likely.

Prednisolone is incorrect. Corticosteroids steroids are used in a wide variety of neuro-inflammatory conditions including such diseases as inflammatory myositis and multiple sclerosis, which may present with weakness. However, the distribution of weakness and clinical findings, in this case, suggest MND. Steroids have no role in the management of this condition.

Pyridostigmine is incorrect. This is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in the management of myasthenia gravis. The weakness in myasthenia is characterized by fatigability, which is not mentioned in this case. Additionally, upper motor neurone signs are not a feature of this condition.

Surgery is incorrect. A cervical radiculomyelopathy (multilevel degenerative disease of the cervical spine) may present with a combination of LMN and UMN signs. Surgery may be indicated in this case. However, these patients typically have neck pain and sensory signs, which are absent in this case, making the diagnosis less likely.

question: A 65-year-old female is admitted with a right hemiparesis. Examination reveals she is in atrial fibrillation. CT confirms an ischaemic stroke and aspirin 300mg is commenced. If the patient is well and develops no new problems at what point should warfarin be started?
options: Following a repeat CT at 28 days to exclude secondary haemorrhage
Following a repeat CT at 14 days to exclude secondary haemorrhage

question: A 34-year-old female with a history of primary generalised epilepsy presents to her GP as she plans to start a family. She currently takes lamotrigine as monotherapy. What advice should be given regarding the prevention of neural tube defects?
options: Folic acid 400 mcg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed
Folic acid 1 mg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed
Folic acid 5 mg per day starting now
Folic acid 10 mg per day starting now
Folic acid 400 mcg per day starting now
correctText: Folic acid 5 mg per day starting now
explanation:
Epilepsy + pregnancy = 5mg folic acid

The correct answer is that folic acid 5 mg per day should be started now. Women taking anti-epileptic medications, including lamotrigine, have an increased risk of having a baby with neural tube defects. The UK epilepsy guidelines recommend that all women with epilepsy who are planning pregnancy should take high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) before conception and continue until the end of the first trimester. This higher dose is necessary because anti-epileptic drugs interfere with folate metabolism. Starting before conception is crucial as neural tube closure occurs very early in pregnancy, often before the woman knows she is pregnant.

Folic acid 400 mcg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed

is incorrect because this is the standard dose recommended for women without risk factors, and waiting until pregnancy is confirmed would be too late to prevent neural tube defects, which develop in the first few weeks after conception.

Folic acid 1 mg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed

is incorrect for the same reasons - the dose is insufficient for women on anti-epileptic medications, and starting after pregnancy confirmation would be too late to provide optimal protection.

Folic acid 10 mg per day starting now

is incorrect because this dose is unnecessarily high and exceeds the recommended dose for women taking anti-epileptic medications. There is no evidence that doses higher than 5 mg provide additional benefit.

Folic acid 400 mcg per day starting now

is incorrect because although the timing of starting before conception is appropriate, this is the standard dose recommended for women without risk factors and is insufficient for women taking anti-epileptic medications who require the higher 5 mg dose.

question:
A 23-year-old man is admitted following the sudden onset of an occipital headache. He initially thought it was a migraine and delayed presenting to the Emergency Department. On examination GCS is 15/15, neurological examination is unremarkable but neck stiffness is noted. He is apyrexial and no rash is noted. A CT scan done 7 hours after symptom onset is normal.

At what time should a lumbar puncture be done?
explanation:
To detect a subarachnoid haemorrhage the LP should be done at least 12 hours after the start of the headache

A lumbar puncture should not be done until 12 hours after the onset of the headache to allow time for xanthochromia to develop.

If the patient was acutely unwell or had an altered GCS then discussion with neurosurgery may be appropriate rather than waiting 12 hours.

question: Which one of the following features is most associated with frontal lobe lesions?
explanation:
Frontal lobe lesions may cause perseveration

The correct answer is

Perseveration

. Perseveration refers to the repetitive and involuntary continuation of a response in the absence of the original stimulus. It is most commonly associated with lesions in the frontal lobe, specifically within the prefrontal cortex. This area is responsible for executive functions including decision making, behaviour regulation, and task flexibility. Damage to this area can disrupt these processes, leading to symptoms such as perseveration.

Wernicke's aphasia

is incorrect as it typically results from damage to Wernicke's area located in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant cerebral hemisphere, which is usually the left hemisphere. This condition is characterised by fluent but nonsensical speech with a lack of comprehension.

Gerstmann's syndrome

, characterised by agraphia (inability to write), acalculia (difficulty with simple mathematical tasks), finger agnosia (inability to distinguish fingers on hand) and left-right disorientation, results from damage to angular gyrus of parietal lobe rather than frontal lobe.

Cortical blindness

arises from bilateral occipital lobe lesions which interrupt visual input to the primary visual cortex. Patients present with loss of vision but may have preserved pupillary light reflex due to intact brainstem pathways.

Lastly,

Superior homonymous quadrantanopia

, also known as 'pie in the sky', results from an infarct in the territory supplied by inferior branch of MCA affecting contralateral inferior parietal lobule or temporal lobe. The lesion here will affect optic radiations carrying information from superior part of visual field resulting in loss of vision in superior quadrant contralaterally. Thus, this condition does not result from frontal lobe lesions.

question: A 59-year-old man presents with a severe pain deep within his right ear. He feels dizzy and reports that the room 'is spinning'. Clinical examination shows a partial facial nerve palsy on the right side and vesicular lesions on the anterior two-thirds of his tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 73-year-old female with a history of recurrent falls at home and alcohol excess is brought to the Emergency Department due to episodes of confusion over the past 5 days. Between these episodes she is apparently her normal self. On examination her GCS is 14/15 and she has nystagmus on left lateral gaze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fluctuating consciousness = subdural haemorrhage

The combination of falls, alcohol excess, fluctuating episodes of confusion and focal neurology points towards a diagnosis of subdural haemorrhage. The phrase 'fluctuating conscious level' is common in questions and should always bring to mind subdural haemorrhage

question:
A 53-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset, severe headache, describing it as the worst of her life. She had been sitting at her desk when the headache came on. She has associated nausea and vomiting.

On examination, she has some neck stiffness and photophobia and appears drowsy. A CT scan shows hyperdense across the basal cisterns and sulci.

Which of the following is indicated in managing the complications of this condition?
explanation:
Nimodipine is used to prevent vasospasm in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhages

The condition being described here is subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), given the sudden-onset severe headache, signs of meningism and CT findings. Nimodipine should be given as a 21-day course to prevent vasospasm - it is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker (CCB) that targets brain vasculature.

Amlodipine is another dihydropyridine CCB but is not used in the management of SAH. It is commonly used as a first-line drug to manage hypertension in those over 55 years old.

Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine CCB and is used in the management of angina and hypertension - as a non-dihydropyridine CCB, it also slows the heart rate. It is not indicated for SAH.

Felodipine, like amlodipine, is another dihydropyridine CCB. It is also used to manage hypertension, but not SAH.

Nifedipine is another dihydropyridine CCB. It can also be used to manage hypertension and is also the first-line treatment for the symptoms of Raynaud's syndrome. It is not indicated for SAH.

question:
A 5-year-old girl has been referred to a paediatric neurologist with frequent episodes which her parents describe as 'daydreaming'. They report that she would suddenly stare blankly into space during a conversation or activity and would be unresponsive for approximately 10-15 seconds. These episodes occur several times a day and she has no recollection of the incidents.

An electroencephalogram (EEG) has been arranged which shows generalised spike-wave activity. Results of blood tests and neuroimaging are unremarkable.

Her parents are concerned about the long-term outlook of her condition.

Based on the seizure type, what is the most likely prognosis?
options: <10% probability of being seizure free in adolescence
25-30% probability of being seizure free in adolescence
45-50% probability of being seizure free in adolescence
70-75% probability of being seizure free in adolescence
90-95% probability of being seizure free in adolescence
correctText: 90-95% probability of being seizure free in adolescence
explanation:
Absence seizures - good prognosis: 90-95% become seizure free in adolescence

The description of this event is very typical of an absence seizure (previously known as petit mal seizure) and is reinforced by the typical EEG findings of generalised spike-wave activity. Many children are treated with ethosuximide or sodium valproate during their childhood years, but the vast majority (90-95%) become seizure-free in adolescence and can be weaned off antiepileptic drugs. This is particularly the case when absence seizures start before the age of 9, as in this patient.

The other percentage options are therefore incorrect.

question:
A 51-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with painless loss of vision in his right eye. This had been preceded by episodes of floaters.

His past medical history included well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he was not on any medications, and a period of poorly-controlled hypertension five years ago, which had culminated in him requiring surgery.

He recalls that his father had died from kidney cancer in his sixties, but is unable to provide any further past medical history.

What is the most likely unifying diagnosis that explains this presentation?
explanation:
Patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome may develop retinal haemangiomas which present as a vitreous haemorrhage

This patient has presented with a vitreous haemorrhage, causing painless loss of vision associated with floaters. Although he is diabetic, his diabetes is well-controlled, and is unlikely to be the cause of his vitreous haemorrhage. The unifying diagnosis is von Hippel-Lindau syndrome - an autosomal dominant condition associated with the development of phaeochromocytomas, retinal and cerebellar haemangiomas, and clear cell carcinomas of the kidney. In this case, a retinal haemangioma has ruptured, causing vitreous haemorrhage. The episode of poorly-controlled hypertension, which was treated with surgery, alludes to a resected phaeochromocytoma, whilst the diagnosis of von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is further supported by his father's death from kidney cancer.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is a plausible risk factor for vitreous haemorrhage. However, there is no description of mucocutaneous telangiectasia in the question, and HHT would not explain the episode of poorly-controlled hypertension, or family history of kidney cancer.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) is associated with phaeochromocytomas, but does not explain the sudden loss of vision or paternal kidney cancer.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 also predisposes to the development of phaeochromocytomas, but there is no suggestion of the classic cutaneous features of cafe-au-lait spots or neurofibromas in this patient.

Neuromyelitis optica can be associated with visual loss due to optic neuritis. However, this is often painful, and associated with other symptoms such as spastic paraparesis or loss of urinary continence.

question: A 17-year-old man is referred to dermatology. He has around 10 hyperpigmented macules on his torso which vary in size from 1.5-5 cm in size. His GP also noted some freckles in the groin region. He is also currently under orthopaedic review due to a worsening scoliosis of the spine. His father suffered from similar problems before having a fatal myocardial infarction two years ago. Which chromosome is most likely to have a gene defect?
explanation:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 - chromosome 17

This patient meets the diagnostic criteria for NF1.

One of our registered users sent the following mnemonic to us:

NF1: chromosome 17 - as neurofibromatosis has 17 characters
NF2: chromosome 22 - all the 2's

question: Lateral medullary syndrome is caused by occlusion of which one of the following blood vessels?
explanation:
Lateral medullary syndrome - PICA lesion - cerebellar signs,  contralateral sensory loss & ipsilateral Horner's

The correct answer to this question is the

Posterior inferior cerebellar artery

. Lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg's syndrome, results from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). This leads to infarction in the lateral part of the medulla oblongata, causing a constellation of symptoms including dysphagia, hoarseness, vertigo, nystagmus, loss of pain and temperature sensation on the ipsilateral face and contralateral body, among others.

Discussing each incorrect option:

Anterior inferior cerebellar artery

: Occlusion here typically results in lateral pontine syndrome rather than lateral medullary syndrome. Symptoms may include facial weakness and sensory loss due to damage to the facial nucleus and tract; hearing loss due to cochlear nuclei damage; ataxia resulting from middle and superior cerebellar peduncle damage; among others.

Posterior cerebral artery

: Occlusion of this artery often leads to occipital lobe infarction with consequent homonymous hemianopia. Other possible symptoms include visual agnosia or memory impairment but not symptoms typical for Wallenberg's syndrome.

Lateral sinus thrombosis

: This condition does not cause lateral medullary syndrome. It is a form of venous sinus thrombosis which can lead to complications such as intracranial hypertension or cerebral venous infarction. Symptoms are usually related to increased intracranial pressure like headache, vomiting and papilledema.

Middle cerebral artery

: Occlusion here causes one of the most common types of ischemic stroke - middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke. This typically presents with contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss (more severe in the face and arm than the leg), homonymous hemianopia and possibly aphasia if dominant hemisphere is affected or neglect if non-dominant hemisphere is affected. These are different from the symptoms seen in Wallenberg's syndrome.

question: A 62-year-old man is referred to the neurology clinic with worsening symptoms over the past few months. The neurologist suspects the patient has progressive supranuclear palsy. Which one of the following features is least likely to be seen in this patient?
explanation:
Progressive supranuclear palsy: postural instability, impairment of vertical gaze, parkinsonism, frontal lobe dysfunction

Impairment of vertical gaze is seen in progressive supranuclear palsy. Horizontal gaze impairment is sometimes seen later as the disease progresses, but would be atypical in a newly diagnosed patient.

question:
A 54-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of memory loss. Her husband states that for a period of 8 hours she was disoriented in time and place, but could remember who she was and was able to recognise family members. She has no recollection of the events. There is no history of any traumatic events. The mental state examination is otherwise normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Transient global amnesia -  acute onset of anterograde amnesia, patent may keep asking the same questions, resolves within 24 hours

The most likely diagnosis is

transient global amnesia (TGA)

which is characterised by the acute onset of anterograde amnesia (the inability to form new memories). It usually resolves within 24 hours.

Dissociation

is incorrect. Dissociation is a mental process where a person disconnects from their thoughts, feelings, memories or sense of identity.

Fugue state

is incorrect. A dissociative fugue is a temporary state where a person has memory loss (amnesia) and ends up in an unexpected place. People with this symptom can't remember who they are or details about their past. The fugue state can last for days, months or longer. The short duration in this case favours a diagnosis of TGA.

Bipolar affective disorder

is incorrect. There are no clinical features (e.g. mania, or delusions) to suggest an underlying bipolar disorder.

Factitious amnesia

is incorrect. A factitious disorder is a condition in which a person, without a malingering motive, acts as if they have an illness by deliberately producing, feigning, or exaggerating symptoms, purely to attain (for themselves or for another) a patient's role. Although this remains within the differential, there is nothing to suggest a factitious disorder in this case.

question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a persistent, generalised headache. He had experienced several episodes of vomiting over the last two days, and remains nauseated.

His past medical history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis, for which he had recently been started on etanercept.

He had received a course of amoxicillin from his GP two weeks previously for a presumed middle ear infection.

During the consultation, he is irritable and easily distracted. On examination, there is no focal neurology, rash, neck stiffness or photophobia.

His observations are as follows: temperature 38.8ºC, respiratory rate 21 breaths per minute, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 135/75mmHg, oxygen saturation 97% on air.

A CT head with contrast is performed, which shows a solitary ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe.

Based on the likely diagnosis, which of the following treatments should be initiated?
explanation:
Brain abscess: IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole

The underlying diagnosis explaining this presentation is a brain abscess. The patient's abscess has likely been caused by intracranial extension of his recent middle ear infection. Brain abscesses are a rare complication of otitis media, and this patient is at an enhanced risk of infection due to immunosuppression from etanercept. The correct option is IV ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, plus metronidazole.

IV piperacillin/tazobactam would be an appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen for sepsis of unknown origin, but the ring-enhancing lesion on contrast CT provides a credible focus of infection in the central nervous system, making targeted therapy more appropriate.

The first-line treatment for a suspected brain abscess is a 3rd-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole. Cefazolin is a 1st-generation cephalosporin, and does not penetrate the central nervous system as successfully as 3rd-generation cephalosporins.

IV aciclovir would be an appropriate initial treatment for suspected viral encephalitis, which may also present with behavioural change and pyrexia. However, the presence of a ring-enhancing lesion on CT points away from this diagnosis.

IV ceftriaxone would be an appropriate antimicrobial treatment for suspected bacterial meningitis in this age group. However, it lacks sufficient anaerobic cover to be used as monotherapy for a brain abscess.

question: A 72-year-old gentleman with a history of hypertension and stroke presents to the emergency department accompanied by his wife. His wife reported him waking at 7am confused. Repetitive questioning was a prominent feature. He was observed to be rubbing his hands together during the event. He was able to recognise his wife and correctly reported his address and date of birth to paramedics. The event lasted approximately 10 minutes. On arrival to the emergency department he a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13 (E3 M6 V4). A full neurological examination was otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which one of the following features is most associated with temporal lobe lesions?
explanation: Temporal lobe lesions may cause auditory agnosia

question: A 45-year-old lady presents with a 2-month history of left-hand weakness. She has no past medical history. On examination, there is a mild weakness of the left upper and lower limbs with a right sided facial weakness which spares the forehead. Where is the lesion?
Which of the following investigations is the most important for diagnosing degenerative cervical myelopathy?
Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the usefulness of cervical spine radiographs (X-rays) in the assessment of degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM)?
options: Cervical spine radiographs should be obtained in all patients suspected of having DCM
Where DCM is suspected, AP (anteroposterior), lateral and oblique cervical spine radiographs should be requested
Cervical spine radiographs are a useful first line investigation where a diagnosis of DCM is suspected
Cervical spine radiographs have a low sensitivity but high specificity for DCM
Cervical spine radiographs cannot diagnose DCM
correctText: Cervical spine radiographs cannot diagnose DCM

question:
A 13-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his concerned parents, who report that over the last month, he has been experiencing multiple episodes of sudden, brief lapses in awareness. These episodes were typically very brief, lasting only a few seconds, during which the boy would stare blankly into space and become unresponsive to his surroundings. He is otherwise well and after the episodes ended, the boy would quickly resume his previous activities, often without any recollection of the lapse in awareness.

Based on the likely diagnosis, what medication is contraindicated in the patient?
explanation:
Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence seizures

This child has presented with features and episodes consistent with absence seizures, often referred to as Petit mal. Absence seizures, characterized by brief lapses in awareness, are thought to result from abnormal electrical activity, particularly spike-and-wave discharges in the thalamus, disrupting thalamocortical circuits and causing temporary cortical inhibition. The condition is typically managed with antiepileptic medication; however,

carbamazepine

is contraindicated in absence seizures due to its mechanism of action. Carbamazepine primarily blocks sodium channels, which are less effective in targeting the thalamocortical circuits responsible for absence seizures. Moreover, carbamazepine can exacerbate absence seizures, likely because of its incompatibility with the spike-and-wave discharges characteristic of these seizures. The drug's mechanism may interfere with normal inhibitory processes in the brain, potentially worsening the condition.

Ethosuximide

is often the first-line choice for treating absence seizures due to its specificity for this seizure type and its ability to effectively control the underlying pathophysiology. Absence seizures are characterised by brief lapses in awareness caused by spike-and-wave discharges in the thalamus, which disrupt thalamocortical circuits and result in temporary cortical inhibition. Ethosuximide's mechanism of action is well-suited to this condition. It acts by blocking calcium channels in neurons, particularly in the thalamus. By doing so, it reduces the abnormal burst firing of neurons that leads to the characteristic spike-and-wave pattern, effectively preventing or minimising absence seizures.

Lamotrigine

is an antiepileptic medication often used as a second-line treatment for absence seizures when other medications like ethosuximide have proven ineffective. It also serves as an alternative to sodium valproate in young females who could potentially become pregnant, thus limiting the risk of congenital issues. Lamotrigine's mechanism of action involves inhibiting excessive neuronal firing by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. While not as specific as some other medications for absence seizures, it can effectively reduce seizure frequency.

Levetiracetam's

exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, but it is believed to modulate neurotransmitter release, potentially reducing excessive neuronal firing. While not the first choice for treating absence seizures, levetiracetam may be considered due to its broad-spectrum antiepileptic properties. However, its use as a second-line treatment depends on individual patient factors and the overall seizure profile. Close monitoring is essential to assess its effectiveness and tolerability.

Sodium valproate

's mechanism of action involves multiple modes, including enhancing the action of inhibitory neurotransmitters, thus regulating excessive neuronal firing. While not typically the initial choice for managing absence seizures, valproate can be effective when primary treatments are unsuitable. However, it's crucial to note that valproate is associated with potential risks during pregnancy, as it can increase the risk of congenital malformations. Therefore, its use in females of childbearing potential should be carefully weighed against the risks, and appropriate contraceptive measures should be taken if it is prescribed.

question: A 54-year-old man with small cell lung cancer complains of muscle weakness. Each one of the following are features of Lambert-Eaton syndrome, except:
options: Repeated muscle contractions lead to decreased muscle strength
correctText: Repeated muscle contractions lead to decreased muscle strength

question: A 49-year-old man is prescribed procyclidine for Parkinson's disease. What is the mechanism of action?
explanation:
Procyclidine - antimuscarinic

The correct answer is

Antimuscarinic

. Procyclidine, a drug commonly used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease, works primarily through an antimuscarinic mechanism of action. It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the central and peripheral nervous system. This results in a reduction of cholinergic activity which helps to balance the dopamine-acetylcholine ratio in the brain, thereby alleviating symptoms associated with Parkinson's disease such as tremors, rigidity and bradykinesia.

The option

Dopamine receptor agonist

is incorrect. While it is true that some drugs used for Parkinson's disease work by directly stimulating dopamine receptors (e.g., pramipexole and ropinirole), procyclidine does not fall into this category. Its primary mechanism of action is antimuscarinic, rather than dopaminergic.

Similarly, the option

Decarboxylase inhibitor

is also incorrect. Decarboxylase inhibitors like carbidopa or benserazide are often given alongside levodopa to prevent its peripheral conversion to dopamine before reaching the brain. However, this is not how procyclidine works.

The option

Dopamine receptor antagonist

would be counterproductive in treating Parkinson's disease. These agents block dopamine receptors and are typically used to treat conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder where there may be an overactivity of dopamine neurotransmission. Using a dopamine antagonist would likely worsen symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Lastly, the option

Monoamine Oxidase-B inhibitor

is also incorrect. While MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline and rasagiline do have a role in managing Parkinson's disease by slowing down the breakdown of dopamine in the brain, this does not describe the mechanism of action for procyclidine.

question: You are called to review a 55-year-old man on the wards who started fitting around 5 minutes ago. He was admitted three days ago following an acute coronary syndrome. His past medical history includes tonic-clonic epilepsy which is generally well controlled on sodium valproate. On your arrival he is still fitting. Oxygen saturations are 99% on 100% oxygen and his pulse rate is 96/min. Intravenous access is already in-situ. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Observe for a further 5 minutes to see if the seizure stops spontaneously
explanation:
IV lorazepam is the first-line treatment in patients with early status epilepticus

As the patient has intravenous access it is most appropriate to give a benzodiazepine parentally due to the more certain absorption.  Lorazepam may be repeated once after 10 minutes.

Intravenous phenytoin is the next line treatment if the seizure fails to stop. Guidelines vary at when this should happen but generally 20-30 minutes is used as a cut-off.

question:
A 23-year-old woman is diagnosed with absence seizures. She is otherwise normally fit and well. A decision is made to initiate treatment. She has recently given birth to her first child and is breastfeeding.

What should be recommended with regards to the management of her seizures?
options: Prescribe carbamazepine and advise her to continue breastfeeding
Prescribe carbamazepine and advise her to stop breastfeeding
Prescribe ethosuximide and advise her to stop breastfeeding
Prescribe lamotrigine and advise her to continue breastfeeding
Prescribe lamotrigine and advise her to stop breastfeeding
correctText: Prescribe lamotrigine and advise her to continue breastfeeding
explanation:
Breast feeding is acceptable with nearly all anti-epileptic drugs

The best answer is to prescribe lamotrigine and advise her to continue breastfeeding. The benefits of breastfeeding are well established and most anti-epileptic drugs are safe in breastfeeding.

For absence seizures, NICE recommend ethosuximide or sodium valproate (except in female patients of child-bearing potential) and if these are unsuitable then lamotrigine can be used.

Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures so should not be prescribed.

Ethosuximide may cause infant sedation when breast-feeding but can be used with care. However, stopping breastfeeding and prescribing ethosuximide would not be the preferred management.

question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with increasing muscle weakness. She reports the weakness mainly affects her shoulders, hips and upper arms. On questioning, she feels her symptoms are worse after a period of inactivity such as sitting and on repeat movement/exercise her weakness actually improves. She confirms she has associated symptoms of a dry mouth and sometimes has difficulty passing urine.

On examination, she has reduced power of the shoulders and upper arms with reduced reflexes throughout. The rest of her examination including peripheral nerve and cranial nerve exam is normal.

What is directly affected in this patient's most likely condition?
explanation:
Lambert-Eaton syndrome - antibodies against the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

This patient has presented with features in keeping with Lambert-Eaton syndrome, a myasthenic syndrome associated with muscle weakness, particularly affecting the limb-girdle region, which generally improves with repetitive contractions. Further features of the condition include hyporeflexia and autonomic disruption such as dry mouth, impotence and difficulty micturating. Lambert-Eaton syndrome is an autoimmune condition due to antibodies directly affecting the presynaptic

voltage-gated calcium channels

in the peripheral nervous system.

Chloride channels

are involved in several regulatory functions within the body including the transport of epithelial fluid in the lung, pancreas and other organs. The main condition associated with chloride channel disruption is the genetic disease cystic fibrosis causing symptoms of mucus thickening and pancreatic insufficiency from birth.

The

myelin sheaths

is affected in several demyelination neurological conditions including multiple sclerosis, transverse myelitis and Guillain-Barre syndrome. In these conditions the myelin surrounding the nerve cell axons is affected, reducing the electrical impulses that are passed along the nervous system. The symptoms seen in these conditions are not improved with repeat use/contractions.

Blockage of the

nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

is the pathophysiology of the neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is a similar autoimmune condition to Lambert-Eaton syndrome causing progressive weakness however MG is normally associated with ocular issues including ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. Also, in contrast to Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeated muscle contraction and activity in MG results in muscle fatigue and a worsening weakness, not an improvement.

Voltage-gated sodium channels

disruption is the pathophysiology in several conditions, in particular neurological syndromes resulting in increased seizure activity such as erythromelalgia and generalised epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) and electrolyte imbalance syndromes such as hyperkalemic and hypokalemic periodic paralysis. The sodium channels are not affected and play no role in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

question:
A 78-year-old right-handed female is admitted with an acute onset stroke of 2 hours duration. The decision was taken by the stroke team for thrombolysis which cures her symptoms. She is subsequently transferred to the high dependency unit for closer monitoring. Overnight, she has three bouts of vomiting and is seen by an FY2 who detects a new onset right-left disorientation and acalculia.

An urgent CT scan is requested which reveals an intracerebral haemorrhage. Which area of the brain is most likely to have been affected?

A 55-year-old female is admitted with a seizure. The seizure fails to respond to repeated dose of intravenous lorazepam. You decide to try a second line agent. Shortly after administration of the drug the patients blood pressure drops to 75/45 mmHg.

What drug is most likely implicated?
explanation:
Intravenous phenytoin can cause hypotension

Intravenous phenytoin can cause hypotension and bradyarrhythmias. Phenytoin is believed to protect against seizures by causing voltage-dependent block of voltage gated sodium channels.  Phenytoin is also a class IB antiarrhythmic drugs which blocks sodium channels in the heart resulting in shortening of repolarization.

question: A 45-year-old female with a past medical history of asthma is diagnosed as having essential tremor. What is the most suitable management?
explanation:
Essential tremor is an AD condition that is made worse when arms are outstretched

Propranolol is generally considered first-line in essential but given the history of asthma primidone should be used

question:
A 76-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of neck stiffness. He complains of numbness in his fingers and difficulty picking up small objects. Recently he has felt increasingly unsteady and had a fall. On examination, he has hyperreflexia in his arms and legs.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
explanation:
Cervical spondylitic myelopathy is caused by advanced osteoarthritis of the cervical spine causing compression of the cervical cord

The most likely diagnosis is cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

All patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy should be assessed by a spinal surgeon. Surgery is recommended in patients with moderate or severe cervical spondylotic myelopathy and in those with disease progression. Treatment of symptoms (for pain, for example) and regular follow-up might be offered for patients with mild, stable cervical spondylotic myelopathy. Decompressive surgery can halt disease progression and improve pain, function, and quality of life. The optimal timing of surgery is debatable because the progression of the disease is poorly understood.

question: A 72-year-old man who is being treated for Parkinson's disease is reviewed. Which one of the following features should prompt you to consider an alternative diagnosis?

A 51-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia is reviewed. He has developed parkinsonism secondary to his antipsychotic medication. Which one of the following drugs is most useful in the management of tremor?

A 30-year-old lady with no past medical history presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of pins and needles in the lower limbs and progressive walking difficulties. She offers a history of a diarrhoeal illness 1 week ago. On examination, there is a loss of pinprick sensation in the lower limbs from mid-thigh distally and in the upper limbs from MCP joints distally. There is a bilateral weakness of ankle dorsiflexion to 3/5 and knee flexion and extension is weak to 4/5 bilaterally. Power in upper and lower limbs is otherwise normal. Knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes are absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 23-year-old man with a history of migraine presents for review. His headaches are now occurring about once a week. He describes unilateral, throbbing headaches that may last over 24 hours. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Other than a history of asthma he is fit and well. What is the most suitable therapy to reduce the frequency of migraine attacks?
explanation:
Migraine

Pizotifen is used less commonly nowadays due to side-effects such as weight gain. Propranolol should be avoided in asthmatics.

question:
A 23-year-old man is brought in by ambulance to the emergency department after having a 5-minute tonic-clonic seizure. He was previously fit and well with no previous seizures. He does not take any regular medication and drinks 5 units of alcohol per week.

Blood tests are unremarkable and a plain CT head has been reported as normal. An EEG is performed and also reported as normal.

A referral to the first seizure clinic has been arranged, but in the meantime, he is worried about the impact on his daily life as he normally drives a car to his office every day, where he works as an accountant.

What is the appropriate advice to give regarding his driving as per the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) guidelines?
options: No driving for 5 years and must notify DVLA
No driving for 6 months and must notify DVLA
No driving for 6 months and no need to notify DVLA
No driving for 12 months and must notify DVLA
No driving for 12 months and no need to notify DVLA
correctText: No driving for 6 months and must notify DVLA
explanation:
Patients cannot drive for 6 months following a first unprovoked or isolated seizure if brain imaging and EEG normal

DVLA guidelines are clear on driving restrictions after a first seizure. For Group 1 (car and motorbike) licence holders, the DVLA must be notified and the driving licence will be taken away. The patient can reapply if he has not had a seizure for 6 months. After that time, the medical advisers will decide if his ongoing risk of another seizure is high enough to warrant further suspension of driving.

It would be incorrect and illegal to not notify the DVLA, as a medical assessment is required at the end of the 6-month period.

A minimum 5-year driving ban would be imposed if this one-off seizure occurred in a Group 2 (bus and lorry) driver.

A 12-month break from driving is excessive, although of course notifying the DVLA would be warranted.

A 12-month break without even notifying the DVLA would be inappropriate.

question:
A 43-year-old woman is referred to the ambulatory care unit with right-sided facial pain, headache and double vision. Symptoms had gradually worsened over the last 2 weeks. She had been well before this.

On examination, ptosis of the right eye is noted. She is also found to have a dilated, unresponsive right pupil. Eye movements of the right eye are also limited - the eye is fixed in a down-and-out position. There is no fatiguability of the ptosis or the eye movements. Neurological examination of the upper and lower limbs is unremarkable.

What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
options: Guillain Barre syndrome - Miller Fisher variant
explanation:
Painful third nerve palsy = posterior communicating artery aneurysm

Posterior communicating artery aneurysm

is correct. This patient is presenting with a third nerve palsy. A 'surgical' (i.e. with pupillary involvement) third nerve palsy suggests a compressive aetiology. This involves compression of the whole nerve and is characterised by a triad of ptosis, pupillary dilatation, and an ophthalmoplegia that leaves the eye in a down-and-out position (due to the unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles). The third nerve palsy with pupil involvement and an associated headache strongly suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm as the cause.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis

is incorrect. A cavernous sinus thrombosis, due to the anatomical proximity to cranial nerves 3, 4, 6 and the ophthalmic branch of 5, usually causes impairment in a mixture of these cranial nerves rather than an isolated 3rd nerve palsy.

Diabetic neuropathy

is incorrect. Patients with vascular risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia can experience peripheral nerve vascular microinfarctions. Diabetic neuropathy affecting the oculomotor nerve would cause a 'medical' (with pupil sparing) third nerve palsy. This would be characterised by ptosis and ophthalmoplegia but would not result in pupillary dilatation. This is because the parasympathetic fibres within the third nerve are found superficially, where the blood supply is primarily from vasa nevorum. In contrast, the somatic muscle fibres supplying levator palpebrae superioris and the extraocular muscles are deep within the third nerve and supplied by intraneural arteries, which are more vulnerable to ischaemic damage.

Guillain Barre syndrome - Miller Fisher variant

is incorrect. Miller Fisher variant can cause a complex ophthalmoplegia that may look like a 3rd nerve palsy, but the ophthalmoplegia is usually bilateral. Miller Fisher variant is also associated with ataxia, areflexia and commonly a prodromal illness - none of which are described in this patient.

Myasthenia gravis

is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis could indeed produce complex ophthalmoplegia and ptosis, but the key differentiating factor is that in myasthenia gravis, these changes would become more pronounced with repetitive movement, a phenomenon known as fatiguability. The symptoms are also usually bilateral, albeit may be asymmetrical.

question:
A 57-years-old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden intense episode of dizziness. Her symptoms began while lying in bed when she turned her head to the side. She experienced two bouts of vomiting accompanied by a sensation that the world was spinning around her.

She has experienced such episodes in the past lasting around 30-60 seconds before self-resolving. Her past medical history is significant for migraines and hypertension. She denies tinnitus or any hearing changes.

Her observations are:

Temperature: 36.9 °C
Blood pressure: 145/90 mmHg
Pulse: 95/min.

Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient's condition?
options: Refer to ears, nose and throat (ENT) specialist
explanation:
The Epley manoeuvre is the treatment of choice for BPPV

This patient has benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), an inner ear disorder leading to a spinning sensation exacerbated by head movement. Canalithiasis (calcium debris) within the semicircular canal leads to the endolymph's improper motion, which results in a spinning sensation. The most appropriate management strategy is to perform canalith repositioning manoeuvre also known as Epley manoeuvre. Epley's manoeuvre involves a stepwise rotation of the head in a way that helps remove the crystals from the semicircular canal.

The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre is used for the diagnosis of BPPV. It leads to vertigo and nystagmus when the affected ear is downwardly turned.

Brandt-Daroff exercises can be used for the treatment of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Since the exercises can cause dizziness, they should be done safely, preferably with another person present. The clinician may perform an Epley manoeuvre in the clinic and then recommend Brandt-Daroff exercises to use at home as these are easier to perform.

Betahistine is a drug that helps to prevent vertigo. It's widely used to treat balance problems or vertigo symptoms, such as those caused by Meniere's disease. In patients with BPPV, who cannot undergo canalith repositioning manoeuvres, betahistine may be considered as a treatment option.

ENT consult may be considered once the patient has stabilised. In most cases, the episode will self-resolve however, treatment with a simple manoeuvre like the Epley can usually stop vertigo right away and thus will be the most appropriate initial management strategy.

question: Each of the following are causes of peripheral neuropathy. Which one is associated with predominately sensory loss?
A 70-year-old man who presented with repetitive large involuntary movements of his right lower limb and right upper limb has been diagnosed with hemiballismus. This affects which part of the brain?
options: Medial thalamus and mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus
Subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia
Substantia nigra of the basal ganglia
Striatum (caudate nucleus) of the basal ganglia
correctText: Subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia
explanation:
Subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia lesions may cause hemiballism

Hemiballism is a type of chorea which is caused by a decreased activity in the subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia in most cases.

The other areas of the brain are associated with other conditions. Wernicke and Korsakoff syndrome localises to the medial thalamus and mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus. Huntington chorea is localised to the striatum (caudate nucleus) of the basal ganglia. Parkinson's disease is caused by disease of the substantia nigra of the basal ganglia. Kluver-Bucy syndrome is caused by damage both temporal lobes including the amygdala.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a 6-month history of progressive weakness in both hands. She mentions accidentally burning her hand on a hot pan without feeling pain. On examination, there is wasting of the small muscles of both hands and reduced pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and upper arms bilaterally, with preserved light touch and vibration sense. Reflexes are brisk in the lower limbs with bilateral upgoing plantars.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Syringomyelia - spinothalamic sensory loss (pain and temperature)

Syringomyelia

is the most likely diagnosis in this case. The patient presents with the classic features of syringomyelia, including dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain and temperature sensation with preservation of light touch and vibration sense) in a 'cape-like' distribution affecting the shoulders and upper arms. This pattern occurs because the expanding syrinx within the spinal cord first affects the crossing spinothalamic tracts in the anterior commissure, which carry pain and temperature sensation, while sparing the dorsal columns that carry light touch, vibration, and proprioception. The history of accidentally burning her hand without feeling pain is particularly characteristic of syringomyelia. Additionally, the patient has upper motor neuron signs in the lower limbs (brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars) and lower motor neuron signs in the upper limbs (wasting of small hand muscles), consistent with a cervical syrinx affecting both anterior horn cells and the corticospinal tracts. Syringomyelia typically presents in young to middle-aged adults and progresses slowly over months to years.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

(ALS) typically presents with a combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs, but without the sensory abnormalities described in this case. ALS would cause progressive muscle weakness and wasting, fasciculations, and upper motor neuron signs such as hyperreflexia and spasticity, but pain and temperature sensation would be preserved. The dissociated sensory loss is not a feature of ALS, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Multiple sclerosis

(MS) can cause a wide variety of neurological symptoms due to demyelination throughout the central nervous system. While MS can cause sensory disturbances, the pattern of dissociated sensory loss described here is not typical. MS lesions tend to cause patchy sensory loss rather than the specific pattern of lost pain and temperature sensation with preserved light touch and proprioception. Additionally, MS typically presents with episodes of neurological dysfunction affecting different parts of the CNS at different times, rather than the progressive course described here.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy

results from spinal cord compression due to degenerative changes in the cervical spine. While it can cause both motor and sensory symptoms in the upper and lower limbs, it typically affects all sensory modalities rather than causing the dissociated sensory loss seen in this case. It is also more common in older patients with evidence of cervical spondylosis, which is not mentioned in this young patient.

Guillain-Barré syndrome

is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy that typically presents with ascending weakness and areflexia. It primarily affects the peripheral nervous system, causing symmetrical weakness, sensory symptoms, and reduced or absent reflexes. The presence of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia and upgoing plantars) in this case rules out Guillain-Barré syndrome, which is characterized by lower motor neuron findings. Additionally, the dissociated sensory loss pattern is not typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

question: A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of visual disturbance. Examination reveals a right incongruous homonymous hemianopia. Where is the lesion most likely to be?

A 28-year-old lady presents with a two-day history of headaches, nausea and vomiting, and blurred vision.

She is long-sighted and has worn glasses since childhood. She has a background of severe migraines and was recently started on a prophylactic medication by her GP.

On examination, both eyes are red with mid-dilated unreactive pupils bilaterally.

Which medication is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Topiramate can precipitate acute angle closure glaucoma

Topiramate is used as a first-line agent in the prophylaxis of migraine. It is an important cause of drug-induced acute angle closure glaucoma, typically occurring within one month of treatment. Topiramate-induced acute angle closure glaucoma is usually treated with cycloplegia and topical steroids alone rather than laser peripheral iridotomy.

Propranolol can be used as a first-line prophylactic treatment for people with episodic or chronic migraine but it is not known to be associated with acute angle closure glaucoma. Adrenergic drugs, in contrast, can precipitate an attack.

Sodium valproate is licensed for migraine prophylaxis though paradoxically itself commonly causes headaches.

Sumatriptan can be used in the in the acute treatment of migraine. It can commonly cause nausea and vomiting, but not angle closure glaucoma.

High-dose aspirin can be used in the acute treatment of migraine. A single dose of 900mg can be taken as soon as the migraine symptoms develop.

question:
A 33-year-old woman is reviewed in the epilepsy clinic. Her epilepsy has been well controlled on carbamazepine 400mg twice daily. She is about to give birth to a baby girl and is very keen to breastfeed.

What should the patient be advised?
options: Breastfeeding should be avoided whilst taking anti-epileptic medication
Increase the dose of carbamazepine by 50%
explanation:
Breast feeding is acceptable with nearly all anti-epileptic drugs

No changes required

is correct. The patient can safely breastfeed whilst taking carbamazepine, or indeed any anti-epileptic medications - except barbiturates.

Breastfeeding should be avoided whilst taking anti-epileptic medication

is incorrect. Most antiepileptic medications are safe to continue in breastfeeding.

Increase the dose of carbamazepine by 50%

is incorrect. This patient's epilepsy is well controlled on the current regimen. A dose increase is unnecessary and could lead to side effects.

Switch carbamazepine to lamotrigine

is incorrect. Her epilepsy is well controlled on the current regimen and a switch would be unnecessary, and no safer.

Switch carbamazepine to levetiracetam

is incorrect. This patient's epilepsy is well controlled on the current regimen. A needless switch in antiepileptic medication could potentially trigger seizures.

question:
A 50-year-old man presents with right-sided ear pain and facial weakness. He had flu-like symptoms of fever and headache for three days before the rash appeared.

On examination, there is a right-sided facial nerve palsy. A vesicular rash is seen on otoscopy.

How should this patient be managed?
explanation:
Treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome consists of oral aciclovir and corticosteroids

The correct answer is oral aciclovir and corticosteroids.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion of the seventh cranial nerve. This patient presents with typical features of the disease including ear pain, facial nerve palsy and a vesicular rash around the ear. Other features include vertigo and tinnitus. Full recovery is more likely if antiviral treatment is started within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms. First-line treatment includes aciclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 7 days and prednisone 60 mg orally daily for 5 days.

Steroids are thought to be helpful in Ramsay-Hunt syndrome due to their strong anti-inflammatory action. This is thought to reduce oedema in the affected nerves and result in shorter disease duration. However, trial evidence supports combining aciclovir and steroids, rather than steroids alone.

Generally, unless the patient is systemically unwell, aciclovir is given orally rather than intravenously for Ramsay-Hunt syndrome.

Steroids are thought to be helpful in Ramsay-Hunt syndrome due to their strong anti-inflammatory action. This is thought to reduce oedema in the affected nerves and result in shorter disease duration. Trial evidence supports combining aciclovir and steroids, rather than steroids alone.

There is evidence that treating Ramsay Hunt syndrome with a combination of oral aciclovir and steroids reduces disease severity and duration, therefore, reassurance alone is an incorrect answer.

question:
A 60-year-old woman with known peripheral vascular disease and atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with acute onset dizziness and alterations in sensation.

On examination, the patient has ataxia and nystagmus. She has left-sided facial numbness and findings in keeping with Horner's syndrome on the same side. The patient has a reduced sensation in both the arm and leg on the right side.

What blood vessel occlusion is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
explanation:
Lateral medullary syndrome - PICA lesion - cerebellar signs,  contralateral sensory loss & ipsilateral Horner's

This patient has presented with features in keeping with a lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg's syndrome. Patients classically presented with both cerebellar and brainstem features as the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, which supplies both areas, is occluded. These features include ataxia and nystagmus (cerebellar features) as well as ipsilateral dysphagia, reduced facial sensation, cranial nerve palsies, and contralateral limb numbness (brainstem features). As this patient's limb sensational changes are on the right side and the facial numbness and Horner's syndrome are on the left it is the

left posterior inferior cerebellar artery

that has been affected. These cross-body findings are key to making the diagnosis.

The

anterior cerebral arteries (ACA)

supply the medial and superior frontal and parietal lobes as well as other structures including the corpus callosum and basal ganglia. Features of ACA strokes can vary but generally present with contralateral weakness of the limbs affecting the leg more than the arm, forms of aphasia and urinary incontinence. Sensory deficits are less common but if present generally affects the contralateral side. Cerebellar and brainstem features are not associated with ACA occlusions.

The

superior cerebellar artery (SCA)

supplies the upper aspect of the cerebellum and parts of the midbrain. SCA infarcts/occlusions result in cerebellar signs including, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, contralateral superficial sensory and nystagmus towards the impaired side (i.e. an infarct of the left superior cerebellar artery will result in left ataxia and nystagmus towards the left). Other general symptoms include hearing loss as well as vertigo, dizziness and mild hemiparesis. Clinical brainstem signs are not commonly associated with SCA strokes.

Patients presenting with posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusions presented with both cerebellar and brainstem features including ataxia and nystagmus (cerebellar features) as well as ipsilateral dysphagia, reduced facial sensation, cranial nerve palsies, and contralateral limb numbness (brainstem features). As this patient's limb sensational changes are on the right side and the facial numbness and Horner's syndrome are on the left it is the left vessel which is affected and not the

right posterior inferior cerebellar artery

.

question:
A 21-year-old man presents with a short history of severe headache, fever and neck stiffness.

An initial CT brain is normal and you proceed to perform a lumbar puncture.

His lumbar puncture results are as follows.


Appearance	Cloudy
Opening pressure	31cmCSF (5 - 20)
WBC count	357 cells/µL (99% polymorphs) (<1)
Glucose	0.4mmol/L (2.5 - 3.5)
Protein	1.3g/L (0.18 - 0.45)

The patient is started on IV antibiotics and steroids and after a few days begins to recover.

He asks you about his prognosis and asks if he is likely to be left with any long-lasting effects of this illness.

What is the most common complication of his condition?
explanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common complication following meningitis

This patient has bacterial meningitis.  His history is suggestive of meningitis and this is confirmed on the lumbar puncture.  He has a high white cell count, high protein and low glucose which are the typical findings of bacterial meningitis.  There is also the high opening pressure and the cloudy CSF which suggest infection.

All of the above options can be complications of meningitis but

sensorineural hearing loss

is the most common, occurring in 34% of cases.

Adrenal insufficiency

is incorrect. It is a rare but recognised complication of meningococcal meningitis and is caused by adrenal haemorrhage.  This is known as Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Conductive hearing loss

is not correct.  Meningitis does not cause conductive hearing loss but does cause sensorineural hearing loss as described above.

Epilepsy

is incorrect.  Ongoing seizures are present following 13% of cases of bacterial meningitis.

Cognitive impairment

is also incorrect as it occurs in about 9% of cases.

It is worth noting complications are more likely with pneumococcal meningitis than in meningococcal meningitis but 57% of those with meningococcal septicaemia will have some form of complication.

question:
A 32-year-old man is brought in following a seizure. His family reports he has been severally unwell the past few days with a fever and vomiting. He was started on antibiotics by his GP last week for suspected bacterial sinusitis following a prolonged period of symptoms including thick nasal mucus and facial discomfort. However, his family confirms he did not complete the antibiotic course.

A CT head with contrast is performed and demonstrates a ring-enhancing lesion with evidence of inflammation of the sinuses.

What antibiotic regime should be commenced?
explanation:
Brain abscess: IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole

This patient has presented with a brain abscess, secondary to spread from an initial sinus infection. Diagnosis is often confirmed via a contrast CT head showing a ring-enhancing lesion that results from the formation of a capsule surrounding the build-up of inflammation and concomitant dead brain tissue. A lumbar puncture is contraindicated due to the risk of potential cerebral herniation. If identified broad-spectrum antibiotics should be commenced immediately. A 3rd generation cephalosporin with additional cover for potential anaerobic and microaerophilic is the recommended regimen such as

IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole

. Dexamethasone should also be considered in patients with evidence of intracranial pressure.

IV ceftriaxone and ampicillin

is mainly used for the management of suspected meningitis in young children, those over 50 years or patients who are immunocompromised. The addition of ampicillin, to the standard 3rd generation cephalosporin, is recommended to cover for potential

Listeria monocytogenes

infection more common in these patient groups. This patient has presented with a brain abscess, not just meningitis, and is not a member of this high-risk patient group.

IV ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole

are not commonly used in combination. Co-trimoxazole, which is made up of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, can cover a range of bacterial, fungal and protozoan infections however it is mainly used as a prophylactic drug to prevent infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis in patients with HIV/AID or other immunosuppressive conditions.

IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin

can be used in combination to treat certain infections such as infective endocarditis or neutropenic sepsis however they are not commonly used for cerebral infections e.g. brain abscess or meningitis.

IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin

should only be considered for brain abscess treatment in countries where cephalosporin resistance is high (e.g. the US) or there is specific reason to suspect specific resistant-infections (e.g. in patient with known methicillin-resistant

Staphylococcus aureus

MRSA).

question: Which one of the following antibodies are associated with painful sensory neuropathy in patients with small cell lung cancer?

You review a 62-year-old man three days after he had been admitted with an acute coronary syndrome. His past medical history includes myasthenia gravis for which he takes long-term prednisolone. Since admission his symptoms of myasthenia have become markedly worse. In particular you notice bilateral ptosis and slurring of speech. Which of the following recently started medications is most likely to be responsible?

A 36-year-old woman presents with a one-hour history of a severe headache. You review her within a few minutes of arrival in the department.

She describes a sudden onset headache and feels it is the worst headache she has ever had in her life. She has felt nauseated since it started and vomited once and also describes photophobia.

Her GCS is 15, she has no focal neurology and is afebrile.

You suspect a subarachnoid haemorrhage and a CT brain is performed one hour after your assessment.

The CT shows no acute intracranial pathology.

What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
If subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected but a CT head done within 6 hours of symptom onset is normal, do

This question tests knowledge of the recent NICE guidelines on the diagnosis and management of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH).

The patient in question has multiple features of SAH and a plain CT brain is the correct initial investigation.

The NICE guidelines suggest that if a patient has a normal CT brain within 6 hours of the onset of the headache then SAH is unlikely and you should

consider an alternative diagnosis

. This is therefore the correct answer.

If the CT is performed greater than 6 hours after the onset of the headache and shows no evidence of SAH then you should consider a

lumbar puncture

, which should be performed at least 12 hours after onset, but this does not apply in this case, so it is incorrect.

If the CT shows a subarachnoid haemorrhage, the next investigation is usually a

CT angiogram

, but this is unnecessary if there is no SAH visible., so is not correct.

If you subsequently do perform a lumbar puncture and this shows xanthochromia, then a

CT angiogram

would then be indicated but is not correct at this stage.

Digital subtraction angiography (DSA)

is incorrect. This is used to determine if an aneurysm is present if a CT angiogram does not identify the cause of the SAH but an aneurysm is still suspected.

Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)

is incorrect and this is only usually performed if DSA is contraindicated.

question:
A 66-year-old man is reviewed in the Neurology clinic after reporting a one-month history of progressive weakness, primarily affecting his upper limbs. He also reports that his limbs feel very stiff in the mornings.

On examination, his movements are 4+/5 bilaterally in his lower limbs, and 3/5 bilaterally in his upper limbs on the Medical Research Council (MRC) power scale. He is also noticed to have a nasal quality to his speech, and occasional calf fasciculations. Peripheral sensation is intact.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following treatment options is most likely to extend this patient's survival?
explanation:
Motor neuron disease - treatment: NIV is better than riluzole

This patient has a diagnosis of motor neuron disease, most likely of the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis subtype. Features consistent with this include his age (onset is most common between ages 55-75), a combination of lower (fasciculations) and upper (upgoing plantars) motor neuron signs, and the classic description of hypernasal speech. Management options for motor neuron disease are limited, with 50% of patients  dying within three years of diagnosis. Of the options above, non-invasive ventilation (NIV) confers the longest survival benefit (on average, 7 months), helping to mitigate type 2 respiratory failure in more advanced disease.

Interferon alpha is used in the treatment of hepatitis C, and has no role in the management of motor neuron disease.

Interferon beta is used in the management of multiple sclerosis relapses. The purely motor nature of the patient's symptoms, presence of lower motor neuron signs and older age of onset ensure that motor neuron disease is a more likely diagnosis than multiple sclerosis in this patient.

Riluzole offers a mild survival benefit in the context of motor neuron disease via down-regulation of GABAergic transmission. However, this benefit is less marked than that offered by NIV.

Chest wall physiotherapy is an important tool in the management of secretions in motor neuron disease. However, its use is not associated with a significant survival benefit, as is the case with NIV.

question:
An 80-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department reporting that he awoke this morning with dizziness and vomiting. On further questioning, you establish that he has a sensation of the room spinning around him, which is worse when he moves his head quickly, although persists with his head still, and that he vomits when these symptoms are at their most severe. He is unsteady on his feet and staggers when you try to walk him around his bed. He has no other symptoms or signs. He has a past medical history of hypertension, high cholesterol, type II diabetes which is diet controlled, and osteoarthritis.

Which of the following diagnoses is it most important to exclude?
explanation:
Posterior circulation stroke must always be considered as a differential in a patient presenting with acute vertigo

A central cause of vertigo must always be considered. Central causes include posterior circulation stroke, acoustic neuroma and other benign and malignant brain tumours, and multiple sclerosis. Stroke is the most urgent diagnosis to make, and the most likely in this patient with cardiovascular risk factors.

A posterior circulation stroke affects the brain tissue supplied by the vertebral, basilar or posterior cerebral arteries - which includes the brainstem, cerebellum, thalamus, midbrain, and parts of the temporal and occipital cortex. Posterior circulation strokes account for 20-25% of ischaemic strokes in the UK but are more difficult to diagnose than anterior circulation strokes. Symptoms can include dizziness, vomiting, double vision, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, limb weakness and visual field defects.
