In subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts are affected

This patient has subacute combined degeneration of the cord which has been precipitated by folic acid supplementation. This patient should have had her vitamin B12 level checked and treated before correcting any folate deficiency to avoid this. Given her demographics, it may be that she has pernicious anaemia (autoantibodies developed against intrinsic factor) and will need intramuscular treatment with vitamin B12. Note that in many B12 deficient patients anaemia develops later than subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

Subacute combined degeneration of the cord affects the dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration sense and tactile discrimination). The tingling that is experienced comes from the effect on the dorsal columns and is often the earliest symptom.

The corticospinal tracts are also affected, causing muscle weakness and hyperreflexia. Patients can also experience spasticity and persistent weakness if the condition is not treated. The Babinski sign and ankle clonus may also be elicited. However, notably, the ankle reflex can often be absent.

Subacute combined degeneration of the cord does not affect the spinothalamic tracts, so the patient would not experience loss of pain and temperature sensation.

Note that symptoms may initially be in the lower limbs or upper limbs, or affect all four limbs coincidently.

question:
A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with left-sided arm weakness and a facial droop. He has a background of hypertension and high cholesterol. His symptoms commenced at 9:30 in the morning. He hoped they would resolve but they have been getting worse. A CT head shows no acute bleed and an area of infarction, and CT angiogram confirms occlusion of the proximal anterior circulation. By the time his imaging is complete, it is now 14:30.

What is the most appropriate management at this stage?
explanation:
The standard target time for thrombectomy in acute ischaemic stroke is 6 hours

NICE has updated stroke guidelines (2019) which now recommend thrombectomy in acute stroke. He is outside the thrombolysis window (4.5 hours) but meets the criteria for thrombectomy (6 hours).

Treatment dose aspirin would be appropriate if he was not suitable for thrombectomy.

Clopidogrel is not suitable as a treatment option in this case but would be used in secondary prevention.

There is no role for DOACs such as edoxaban in the management of acute stroke. DOACs may be used in the management of AF if this is found, but are not generally started until later.

question: A 35-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia is brought to the Emergency Department by worried friends due to drowsiness. On examination he is generally rigid. A diagnosis of neuroleptic malignant syndrome is suspected. Each one of the following is a feature of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, except:

A 45-year-old man is investigated for spastic leg weakness which has come on over the previous 5 days.

He undergoes a whole spine MRI which shows:

Hyperintense T2 signal extending across the spinal cord, between the levels of T9 and T12.


Which of the following is most likely to cause this clinical and radiological presentation?
explanation:
Transverse myelitis can be caused by viral infection - such as varicella, herpes simplex, EBV and HIV

The radiographical features are descriptive of transverse myelitis -inflammation across most of the spinal cord.

One notable cause is viral infections (including HIV).

Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndrome are lesions of the lumbar region of the spinal cord.

Diabetes is not well documented to cause transverse myelitis.

Brown-Sequard syndrome is caused by a lesion of one half of the spinal cord only.

question:
A 55-year-old presents to the emergency department with a rash. He has felt feverish for the preceding three days. His past medical history includes epilepsy, hypertension, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and rheumatoid arthritis. His medications include aspirin, hydralazine, furosemide, lamotrigine and methotrexate.

His observations are heart rate 111 beats per minute, blood pressure 93/55 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air and temperature 38.1ºC.

On examination there are widespread blisters on his skin, some of which have burst, leaving painful sores. The mucus membranes are affected with ulceration of the mouth, throat and genital tract. Approximately 10% of his body surface area is affected.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of his medications is the likely cause?
explanation:
A rare but recognised adverse effect of lamotrigine therapy is Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Lamotrigine is the correct answer. The patient has Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) as evidenced by a flu-like illness with fevers followed by subsequent blistering and ulcerating skin lesions involving the body and mucus membranes. The most likely cause from his list of medications is lamotrigine.

Furosemide is incorrect. This can cause bullous skin eruptions and there have been a few case reports of it causing SJS but it is a much less likely cause than lamotrigine.

Hydralazine is incorrect. This is a classic cause of drug-induced lupus.

Aspirin is incorrect. This is not associated with the development of SJS. It is the 'oxicam' class of anti-inflammatory drugs (including meloxicam and piroxicam) that are associated with the development of SJS.

Methotrexate is incorrect. It is another DMARD (sulfasalazine) that is associated with the development of SJS in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

question: A 23-year-old woman undergoes a planned lumbar puncture (LP) as part of neurological investigations for possible multiple sclerosis. During the consent process, she expresses concern about a post-LP headache. What is the mechanism of post-LP headaches?
options: Leaking cerebrospinal fluid from the dura
correctText: Leaking cerebrospinal fluid from the dura

question:
A 45-year-old male with a history of alcoholic liver disease presents with increasing confusion. On assessment, he is noted to be obtunded with a Glasgow coma scale of 14 out of 15, has a wide-based gait and nystagmus. There is no history or signs of recent trauma.

What is the most specific finding on brain MRI for this patient's condition?

A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a five-day history of fever, malaise, upper respiratory tract symptoms and painful skin. She then developed a dark red target pattern rash which has spread from the torso and upper limbs to involve her distal limbs, face, palms and soles.

She has recently been diagnosed with epilepsy and started on anti-convulsant medication.

On examination, there are widespread purpuric macules and confluent areas of erythema. There are scattered blisters and skin erosions including on her mucous membranes and labia. Gentle lateral pressure causes detachment of the epidermis.

Which medication is the most likely to have caused the presentation?
explanation:
A rare but recognised adverse effect of lamotrigine therapy is Stevens-Johnson syndrome

The correct answer is lamotrigine.

This woman has presented with Stevens-Johnson syndrome. While the BNF lists severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR) under most anticonvulsants/anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs), patients who experience AED-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) will still require ongoing treatment for their epilepsy with an option that minimises the risk of SJS. The greatest risk is with aromatic AEDs such as phenytoin, phenobarbital and carbamazepine, but lamotrigine is also a well-recognised cause.

There may be an issue with over-reporting / over-diagnosis of SCAR and SJS in patients taking AEDs due to an awareness of the possibility for reactions.

Newer studies suggest that sodium valproate, gabapentin, pregabalin, levetiracetam, topiramate, clonazepam and ethosuximide are lower risk for SJS.

The other listed drugs can cause a range of other side effects.

Gabapentin can cause lethargy, nausea and vomiting, mood changes, blurred vision and dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, weight gain, headaches and memory impairment. It has been associated with a risk of severe respiratory depression even without concomitant opioids.

Levetiracetam commonly causes drowsiness, headaches, nausea and vomiting. Levetiracetam has been associated with renal impairment and behavioural change including increased risk of suicidal thoughts.

Sodium valproate commonly causes nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea, tremors, headache, weight gain, thinning hair and irregular menses. It is also teratogenic - women of childbearing potential should use highly effective contraception during treatment.

Topiramate commonly causes nausea, lethargy, diarrhoea, mood change and weight loss. It is importantly associated with risk of glaucoma, renal stones, metabolic acidosis and reduced sweating. It should be avoided in acute porphyrias.

question:
A 55-year-old man presents with word-finding difficulties which came on suddenly one hour ago. He is not able to give a meaningful response to any of your questions. He is unable to name simple objects and the output of spontaneous speech is markedly diminished. You ask him to touch his left ear lobe with his right index finger which he manages without issue.

What area of the brain is affected?
explanation:
Broca's dysphasia: speech non-fluent, comprehension normal, repetition impaired

Inferior frontal gyrus

is correct.  The patient has Broca's dysphasia characterised by non-fluent speech but normal comprehension. The patient is able to follow complex commands indicative of normal comprehension. Broca's dysphasia occurs due to a lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus.

Lateral geniculate nucleus

is incorrect. This is a component of the thalamus which is a very important component of the visual pathway. A lesion of this nucleus produces moderately to completely congruent visual field defects.

Medial geniculate nucleus

is incorrect. The medial geniculate nucleus is part of the auditory thalamus and represents the thalamic relay between the inferior colliculus and the auditory cortex. Although the medial geniculate nucleus is a well-known integration centre for the central auditory pathways, auditory symptoms caused by damage to these nuclei are rarely described. However, there are some case reports of auditory hallucinations.

Striate cortex

is incorrect. This is the part of the brain which deals with the processing of signals from the visual pathway. Lesions of the striate cortex can result in blindness.

Superior temporal gyrus

is incorrect. Wernicke's aphasia occurs due to a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus.  In Wernicke's aphasia, the ability to grasp the meaning of spoken words and sentences is impaired. Patients with Wernicke's aphasia speak normal words fluently, often including meaningless phonemes, but do not know their meaning or relationships. The result is a jumble of words or 'word salad'. Patients are typically unaware that their speech is incomprehensible to others.

question:
A 42-year-old woman presents describing a sudden onset of visual disturbances, including blurred vision. She has also noticed increasing numbness and tingling in her right arm and leg over the past few days.

On examination, neurological findings revealed weakness, hyperreflexia, and impaired coordination. A diagnosis of possible multiple sclerosis is suspected and so an MRI is performed demonstrating hyperintense lesions perpendicular to the corpus callosum (i.e. Dawson fingers).

What MRI sequence has most likely been performed?
explanation:
Use MRI FLAIR sequence in diagnosis of multiple sclerosis vs. MRI STIR in flares of thyroid eye disease

Dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI

sequence is commonly used in oncology management and involves the administration of a contrast agent during imaging to assess blood flow and tissue permeability. Unlike static MRI sequences, DCE provides a dynamic view of contrast distribution especially valuable in oncology, as it helps evaluate tumour vascularity and guide treatment planning. DCE-MRI's ability to depict changes in tissue perfusion and capillary permeability enhances its role in understanding and describing the features of lesions, monitoring treatment response, and contributing to precise diagnoses in various medical contexts.

MRI short tau inversion recovery (STIR)

sequence selectively nullifies signals from fat, enhancing the visibility of pathological tissues. Unlike traditional sequences, STIR employs a short inversion time, suppressing the fat signal and emphasising water-based tissues. This makes it particularly useful for imaging musculoskeletal structures, joints, and soft tissues such as in thyroid eye disease (TED). In TED, STIR helps visualise soft tissue changes, inflammation, and oedema around the eye, aiding with assessing disease severity and guiding management.

T1-weighted (T1W) MRI

sequence highlights differences in the relaxation times (the time it takes for the nuclear magnetic spins within tissues to return to their equilibrium state) of tissues, producing images with distinct anatomical contrast. While T1W sequences are valuable for anatomical imaging, they have limited sensitivity to MS-related changes.

T2-weighted (T2W) MRI

sequence accentuates differences in tissue water content and is particularly adept at highlighting pathology. Its primary uses include detecting oedema, inflammation, and lesions, making it invaluable in neurological and musculoskeletal imaging. However, compared to FLAIR sequences, T2W is less effective in suppressing the signal from cerebrospinal fluid, often leading to reduced lesion conspicuity in certain scenarios, especially in neurological conditions like MS where FLAIR sequences are preferred for enhanced lesion visualisation.

question: A 31-year-old female with progressive leg weakness has nerve conduction studies for suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which one of the following findings would be most consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Extended series of repetitive discharges lasting up to 30 seconds

question:
A 32-year-old nursery teacher complains of progressive hearing loss and tinnitus over the past three months. She denies aural fullness and recent infections. The patient recalls that her mother was diagnosed with a 'hearing problem' in her thirties.

External examination of the ear is normal. Rinne test: bone conduction is louder than air conduction in both ears. Weber test: sound localised to the centre of the forehead.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Otosclerosis is characterised by conductive hearing loss, tinnitus and positive family history

Rinnes test is positive when air conduction is better than bone conduction. This is seen in normal examinations or when patients have sensorineural hearing loss. A negative test signifies conductive hearing loss. This patient has bilateral negative Rinnes test, therefore she is likely to have bilateral conductive hearing loss. The positive family history also suggests otosclerosis as the most likely diagnosis. It is a condition caused by abnormal bone remodelling of the middle ear.

Labyrinthitis

is inflammation of the labyrinth. Symptoms include vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus. They usually resolve within a week. The symptoms described here have been ongoing for a few months.

Cholesteatoma

causes ear infection and discharge, with unilateral conductive hearing loss, instead of bilateral conductive hearing loss seen in otosclerosis.

Meniere's disease

is characterized by unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, in which case sound lateralizes towards the contralateral normal ear during the Weber test. The patient also does not have other convincing features of Meniere's disease such as tinnitus, aural fullness, and vertigo attacks. In addition, the positive family history in this stem suggests an inherited disorder such as otosclerosis, whereas most cases of Meniere's disease are sporadic.

Vestibular schwannoma

presents as unilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Patients would also have facial nerve palsies, vertigo, and ataxia.

question: You are called to see a 62-year-old female inpatient, with a known history of epilepsy, who is having a seizure. The nurse who witnessed the seizure says it began by affecting her right hand before involving her entire right arm and then progressing to a loss of consciousness with her entire body shaking. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 55-year-old woman with a background of metastatic breast cancer presents with a short history of nausea and vomiting. She has vomited five times today, despite taking regular metoclopramide. She received palliative chemotherapy three days ago.

You decide to commence treatment with ondansetron.

What is the best description of the mechanism of action of this medication?
explanation:
Ondansetron is a 5-HT 3 serotonin antagonist

Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 serotonin antagonist, which blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system, and specifically at the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). It is particularly effective for chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting and is often used first line in this setting. However, constipation is a very common side-effect and so laxatives should usually be co-prescribed.

5-HT1 agonists are used in the acute management of migraine. Examples include sumatriptan and rizatriptan.

5-HT2 antagonists are used for migraine prophylaxis, however their use is limited by side effects:

Pizotifen: weight gain and drowsiness
Methysergide: retroperitoneal fibrosis

Dopamine antagonists are also used in the management of nausea and vomiting. These include antipsychotic medications such as haloperidol and levomepromazine, as well metoclopramide and domperidone. Metoclopramide  acts directly on the gastro-intestinal tract and is useful to treat nausea and vomiting associated with gastroduodenal, hepatic, and biliary disease. However, it should be used with caution in young women as it may induce an acute dystonic reaction such as oculogyric crises in this group.

H1 (histamine) antagonist is incorrect. Cyclizine is an example of a H1-antagonist, which is effective in treating nausea and vomiting resulting from many underlying conditions.

question: A 67-year-old male undergoes investigations for bilateral paraesthesia in the radial aspects of both hands, over the thumbs and first fingers. He also has paraesthesia in the lateral aspects of both forearms and lower limb spasticity. Blood tests reveal a HBA1c of 46 mmol/mol. He undergoes nerve conduction studies and EMG with evidence of denervation. Which ONE of the following diagnoses is most likely?

A 23-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department following a close-range gunshot wound to the head from a handgun. The bullet entered the side of the patient's skull, resulting in a small entrance wound with no exit wound.

A CT scan of the head is conducted, confirming isolated penetration and consequent damage to the parietal lobe. He undergoes neurosurgical intervention to remove the bullet.

What condition may be associated with this lesion?
explanation:
Parietal lobe lesions may cause astereognosis

The parietal lobe, situated near the top and towards the rear of the brain, is one of the four major cerebral lobes. Damage or lesions in this lobe can occur due to various factors, such as stroke, tumours, infections, and, as seen in this case, trauma. The parietal lobe plays a pivotal role in processing sensory information, spatial awareness, and the integration of sensory inputs to create a comprehensive perception of the surrounding environment. Individuals with parietal lobe lesions may develop multiple deficits, including a condition called

astereognosis

, which involves the inability to recognise or identify objects through the sense of touch. This impairment typically arises due to damage to the somatosensory cortex, located within the parietal lobe, responsible for processing tactile information originating from different parts of the body.

Anosmia

, the loss or reduction of the sense of smell, typically results from frontal lobe lesions, not parietal. The frontal lobes are critical for processing sensory information, including olfactory (smell) signals. These lobes integrate smell with other cognitive functions, such as memory and emotion. When damaged, typically due to trauma, tumours, or medical conditions, the processing of smell is disrupted.

Expressive aphasia

, also known as Broca's aphasia, is a language disorder arising from frontal lobe lesions in the brain. Specifically, damage to Broca's area, situated in the left frontal lobe (typically for right-handed individuals), is the underlying cause. This region controls the motor aspects of speech production, orchestrating the precise muscle movements needed for articulate speech. Consequently, when frontal lobe lesions occur, particularly in or near Broca's area, it disrupts the ability to form and express words and sentences fluently. This leads to non-fluent, halting speech characterised by difficulties in word retrieval and constructing coherent sentences, while language comprehension remains relatively intact.

Perseveration

is a cognitive phenomenon where an individual continues to repeat a particular behaviour, word, or thought even when it is no longer relevant or appropriate. This often occurs in the context of frontal lobe lesions in the brain. The frontal lobes are responsible for executive functions, including cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control. Damage to this region can disrupt the brain's ability to switch between tasks or responses and inhibit irrelevant actions or thoughts.

Wernicke's aphasia

, often referred to as 'fluent aphasia,' is a language disorder marked by fluent yet incoherent speech and profound difficulties in language comprehension. This condition arises from lesions or damage to Wernicke's area, typically located in the left temporal lobe, specifically the superior temporal gyrus. Wernicke's area is pivotal for processing and comprehending language. When damaged, it disrupts the brain's ability to interpret and formulate coherent speech, resulting in sentences that flow smoothly but lack meaningful content. Individuals with Wernicke's aphasia often use invented or inappropriate words, rendering their speech unintelligible. Their comprehension of spoken and written language is severely compromised, leading to significant communication challenges.

question: Which one of the following features is most likely to be seen following facial nerve paralysis?
Each of the following features are seen in myotonic dystrophy, except:
explanation:
D

The correct answer is

Round face

. Myotonic dystrophy (DM) is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder characterised by myotonia, progressive muscle weakness, and involvement of multiple organ systems. Patients with myotonic dystrophy typically present with a distinctive facial appearance, but this is characterised by a long, thin face with temporal wasting and ptosis, not a round face. The facial appearance is often described as 'hatchet-faced' due to the wasting of the temporalis and masseter muscles, along with weakness of facial muscles.

Mild mental impairment

is indeed a feature of myotonic dystrophy, particularly in congenital and childhood-onset forms. Cognitive impairment in myotonic dystrophy can range from mild learning difficulties to more significant intellectual disability. Executive dysfunction, visuospatial deficits, and attention problems are commonly observed cognitive features.

Frontal balding

is a characteristic feature of myotonic dystrophy, particularly in males. This premature frontal balding (frontal alopecia) is one of the recognisable physical manifestations of the condition and contributes to the distinctive facial appearance of affected individuals.

Myotonia

is the hallmark feature of myotonic dystrophy, from which the condition derives its name. Myotonia refers to delayed muscle relaxation after contraction, which clinically manifests as muscle stiffness. Patients often describe difficulty releasing their grip after a handshake or may demonstrate the phenomenon when asked to make a fist and then rapidly open their hand. This feature can be objectively demonstrated by percussion myotonia, where tapping a muscle (commonly the thenar eminence) results in a delayed relaxation.

Cataracts

are a common ocular manifestation of myotonic dystrophy. These are typically posterior subcapsular iridescent cataracts, which may be detected on slit-lamp examination before they become visually significant. Cataracts can sometimes be the presenting feature of myotonic dystrophy, particularly in milder forms of the condition, and may develop at a relatively young age compared to age-related cataracts.

Other important features of myotonic dystrophy not mentioned in the options include cardiac conduction abnormalities, endocrine disturbances (such as insulin resistance and testicular atrophy), respiratory muscle weakness, excessive daytime sleepiness, and gastrointestinal symptoms. The condition exists in two main forms: myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), caused by a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the DMPK gene, and myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2), caused by a CCTG tetranucleotide repeat expansion in the CNBP gene.

question: Which one of the following side-effects is least associated with the use of levodopa?

You are asked to see a 21-year-old woman on the medical take who presents with a 2-day history of blurred vision and pain in her right eye which worsened after her morning bath. She had similar symptoms 6 months ago affecting her right eye but these resolved spontaneously and she did not seek medical attention. Examination reveals a central scotoma and impaired colour vision on Ishihara plates in the right eye. Examination is otherwise unremarkable. A contrast MRI brain shows T2 enhancement of the right optic nerve but no other abnormalities. Lumbar puncture demonstrates oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Her mother has multiple sclerosis (MS) and she is understandably anxious to discuss her diagnosis and treatment options. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure her she does not have MS and discharge
Give steroids and arrange MRI whole spine
Give steroids and arrange repeat MRI brain as a neurology outpatient
correctText: Give steroids and arrange MRI whole spine
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis diagnosis that requires demyelinating lesions that are separated in space and time

The diagnosis of multiple sclerosis requires the identification of demyelinating lesions that are separated in space and time. The question is trying to lure you into making a diagnosis of MS but pay attention to the details and don't be fooled- on the evidence provided you cannot demonstrate that lesions are separated in BOTH space and time and so you can't diagnose MS.

She currently has optic neuritis affecting the right eye. This is supported by the MRI brain showing a demyelinating lesion of the right optic nerve. From her history it's likely she has had a previous episode of right-sided optic neuritis. So she has disease separated in time but so far not space. Oligoclonal bands in the CSF help support a diagnosis of MS but aren't diagnostic and still don't show dissemination in space. For this she would need to have a contrast-enhanced MRI spine. This could show old plaques/active demyelination; that would confirm disease disseminated in time AND space and so allow a diagnosis of MS.

Giving steroids to treat her optic neuritis can shorten the duration of the attack and improve recovery so it's appropriate to start them.

1 - Beta-interferon is used in certain MS patients who meet specific criteria. It reduces the frequency of attacks. It is inappropriate to start in this scenario as you are not even able to confirm a diagnosis of MS

2 - You cannot exclude MS with the information available and so it would be wrong (and frankly negligent) to reassure and discharge her (on the basis of probability it's very likely that she has/will develop MS in the future but again on the limited information you have available you can't make that diagnosis).

3 - This is the best option. By doing an MRI spine you can determine if there are lesions separated in space and time. Steroids would treat her current optic neuritis

4. Visual evoked potentials are used in investigating MS but wouldn't add anything in this scenario. You already know she has optic neuritis and the MRI brain has shown a demyelinating lesion.

5 - Giving steroids would help her current optic neuritis but simply repeating the MRI brain at a later date is inappropriate

question: A 71-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department. His family report that since yesterday he has been very 'clumsy' and unsteady on his feet. This morning he started to complain of numbness down his left side. On examination you notice that he has a right-sided Horner's syndrome and horizontal nystagmus. Examination of the peripheral nervous system confirms the sensory loss on the left side. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
Each one of the following is associated with Friedreich's ataxia, except:
options: Increased risk of deep vein thrombosis
correctText: Increased risk of deep vein thrombosis

question: A 67-year-old male attends the Emergency department with sudden onset dizziness and vomiting, which has been present for the past 2 hours. He has a background of hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia for which he takes ramipril and simvastatin. Examination reveals vertical nystagmus and difficulty standing without support. What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management?

A 23-year-old man with difficult to control epilepsy is reviewed in clinic, four months after a change in his antiepileptic medication. He has remained seizure free but has gained 5 kg in weight since last reviewed. Which one of the following antiepileptic drugs is most associated with weight gain?
explanation:
Sodium valproate may cause weight gain

The correct answer is

sodium valproate

, as it is the antiepileptic drug most commonly associated with weight gain. Sodium valproate can cause weight gain by increasing appetite and altering metabolism. This side effect is particularly concerning in patients who are already overweight or at risk of obesity-related medical conditions.

Ethosuximide

is typically used for absence seizures and is not commonly associated with significant weight gain. It may cause gastrointestinal side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, but these usually do not contribute to changes in body weight.

Levetiracetam

has a relatively neutral effect on body weight. Some patients may experience mild weight gain or loss, but this is generally not a major concern when prescribing this medication.

Carbamazepine

can actually lead to modest weight loss in some patients due to its potential gastrointestinal side effects, such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. However, these side effects are usually transient and subside after an initial period of treatment.

Finally,

lamotrigine

also has a relatively neutral effect on body weight. It may cause mild fluctuations in appetite but does not typically result in significant weight gain or loss.

question:
A 72-year-old man presents to the Medical Assessment Unit with a 3-week history of intermittent confusion and mild right-sided weakness. His wife reports he has become increasingly forgetful and unsteady on his feet. There is no clear history of trauma. On examination, he has subtle right-sided pronator drift and mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 23/30). A CT head is performed.

What is the most likely radiological finding?
options: Bilateral hyperdense collections in the frontal regions
Hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral convexity
Hyperdense lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding oedema
Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci
correctText: Hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral convexity
explanation:
On CT imaging, a chronic subdural haematoma will appear as a hypodense (dark), crescentic collection around the convexity of the brain

Hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral convexity

is the correct answer. This patient's presentation is highly suggestive of a chronic subdural haematoma (CSDH). The gradual onset of confusion, progressive neurological deficit (right-sided weakness), and cognitive impairment over weeks are classic features. The right-sided weakness indicates a left-sided lesion (contralateral to the deficit). On CT imaging, a CSDH typically appears as a hypodense (dark), crescent-shaped collection that follows the convexity of the brain. The hypodensity develops as the haematoma ages over weeks, with protein breakdown and increased fluid content. CSDHs are common in elderly patients due to age-related brain atrophy creating tension on bridging veins, which can tear with even minor (and sometimes unnoticed) trauma.

Bilateral hyperdense collections in the frontal regions

would be more consistent with acute subdural haematomas, which appear hyperdense (bright) on CT due to the presence of fresh blood. Acute subdurals typically present with a more rapid onset of symptoms following a clear history of trauma, rather than the gradual progression seen in this case. Additionally, bilateral frontal collections would likely produce different neurological deficits than the unilateral right-sided weakness described.

Hyperdense lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding oedema

describes the appearance of an intracerebral haemorrhage or tumour. This is an intra-axial (within brain tissue) rather than extra-axial lesion. While this could cause right-sided weakness, the acute onset and rapid progression would be more typical for an intracerebral haemorrhage, and the surrounding oedema pattern is more characteristic of a tumour or subacute haemorrhage, neither of which fit the clinical timeline.

Enlarged ventricles with periventricular lucency

describes findings consistent with normal pressure hydrocephalus or obstructive hydrocephalus. While normal pressure hydrocephalus can present with cognitive impairment and gait disturbance (part of the classic triad along with urinary incontinence), it typically doesn't cause focal weakness and would affect both sides equally.

Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci

is a finding associated with neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease or other dementias. While this could explain the cognitive impairment, it would not account for the focal right-sided weakness or the relatively rapid progression of symptoms over just three weeks.

question: A 19-year-old female presents complaining of visual disturbance. Examination reveals a bitemporal hemianopia with predominately the lower quadrants being affected. What is the most likely lesion?
explanation:
Bitemporal hemianopia

Craniopharyngioma

is indeed the correct answer. Craniopharyngiomas typically arise from remnants of Rathke's pouch above the pituitary gland and compress the optic chiasm from above. This superior compression characteristically causes a bitemporal hemianopia that affects the inferior fields first (as the crossing fibers in the superior chiasm are compressed first), which matches the description in this case. These tumors commonly present in children or young adults.

Brainstem lesion

is incorrect as brainstem lesions typically cause cranial nerve palsies, long tract signs, or internuclear ophthalmoplegia rather than visual field defects.

Frontal lobe lesion

is incorrect as frontal lobe lesions do not typically cause visual field defects unless they extend posteriorly to involve the optic radiation.

Pituitary macroadenoma

is incorrect because while it can cause bitemporal hemianopia, it typically grows upward from below the chiasm and affects the superior visual fields first (opposite to this case).

Right occipital lesion

is incorrect as this would cause a left homonymous hemianopia rather than a bitemporal defect. Occipital lesions affect the contralateral visual field and do not cause bitemporal defects.

The key to this question is recognizing that a bitemporal hemianopia affecting inferior fields first strongly suggests compression of the optic chiasm from above, which is characteristic of craniopharyngioma.

question:
A patient presenting to the emergency department undergoes a CT head scan. The report describes a hypodense collection around the convexity of the brain that is not limited to suture lines.

What is the most likely radiological diagnosis?
explanation:
On CT imaging, a chronic subdural haematoma will appear as a hypodense (dark), crescentic collection around the convexity of the brain

On CT imaging, acute haematomas appear bright (hyperdense) whereas chronic haematomas appear dark (hypodense). Extradural haematomas are limited by suture lines whereas subdural haematomas are not. Intraparenchymal haematomas arise within the brain substance. Subarachnoid haemorrhage are typically seen as hyperdensity within the basal cisterns and sulci of the subarachnoid space.

question:
A 31-year-old man attends his appointment with an oncologist after being referred by his family physician. The man reported feeling nauseous and having a persistent headache for the past month. The pain was not relieved by the regular over-the-counter painkiller. The patient confirms that he has a significant family history of cancer and this is why he has been referred to see the oncologist.

After chromosome analysis which revealed an abnormality related to the chromosome 3p, the patient is explained that his condition will put him at higher risk of developing several tumors, which could be both benign and malignant. The oncologist tells the patient that this condition can be passed on to future generations and that the patient's children have a fifty-percent chance of developing the condition, given his spouse does not carry the mutation as well. The patient is happy to know that he will not need a screening flexible sigmoidoscopy.

Which of the following diseases is the patient at the highest risk of developing due to his underlying condition?
explanation:
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is associated with the development of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma

This patient presented with a persistent headache and feeling nauseous, in the setting of a positive family history of cancer. This has prompted the family physician to make a referral to an oncologist for further investigations. An abnormality related to the chromosome 3p, which carries the VHL gene, indicates that this man might be suffering from Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome. This is an autosomal dominant condition which increases the risk of developing several cancers. Clear-cell renal carcinoma is one of the tumors which patient with VHL syndrome are at an increased risk of suffering from, although the most common tumors are hemangiomas. None of the other cancers mentioned below are associated with VHL although they may occur in a person with VHL.

(First Aid 2017, p495).

1: Lung carcinoma is one of the major causes of death worldwide. The disease is mainly due to smoking but can also occur in non-smokers due to environmental pollutants. Symptoms include persistent cough, hemoptysis, and loss of weight. Chest X-ray is an important first-line investigation in patients suspected of having lung cancer.

3: Prostate carcinoma is one of the most common cancers in men. Patients usually present with lower urinary tract symptoms such as frequency, poor flow or nocturia amongst others. While these symptoms are often due to benign prostatic hypertrophy, it is important to investigate these patients to rule out a prostate malignancy.

4: Breast carcinoma is one of the most common cancers in women. It can be non-invasive or invasive. Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common of all breast cancers. Treatment range from wide-margin excision to mastectomy, and may also include radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

5: Osteogenic sarcoma, also known as osteosarcoma, is one of the most prevalent bone tumors of malignant origin. The disease usually occurs into those under 20 years and above 65 years of age. Anatomically, it develops in the metaphyses of the long bones, typically around the knee. A characteristic X-ray appearance is that of the Codman triangle.

question:
A 35-year-old male patient with a past medical history of adult polycystic kidney disease is admitted to hospital with a sudden-onset, severe occipital headache associated with nausea and vomiting. He rates the severity of his headache as 10/10 and describes it as 'the worst headache of his life.'

Vital signs are notable for a heart rate of 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 135/70 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and temperature of 37.0ºC.

On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 14/15, pupils are symmetric in size and reactive to light, and there are no focal neurological deficits.

A non-contrast Computed Tomography (CT) scan of his head reveals the suspected diagnosis.

While awaiting further management in the Emergency Department a few hours after symptom onset, he develops an acute deterioration in his neurological status with a GCS drop to 11/15. Haemodynamic parameters remain within normal range.

Given the suspected complication in question, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Subarachnoid haemorrhage: if rebleeding is suspected (e.g. sudden worsening of neurological symptoms) → repeat CT

The syndrome described in the vignette is that of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) likely secondary to a berry aneurysm in a patient with adult polycystic kidney disease. Complications of SAH include, among others, re-bleeding, vasospasm with delayed cerebral ischaemia, hydrocephalus, seizures, hyponatraemia, and cardiopulmonary complications.

One of the early complications is re-bleeding, which may occur as early as 2-12 hours following the bleeding event, marked by a sudden deterioration in the patient's neurological symptoms. If re-bleeding is suspected, patients should have an urgent repeat CT Head to confirm this. Re-bleeding is associated with a high mortality rate and patients with rebleeding should undergo emergency repair of their aneurysm.

Transcranial dopplers can be used to evaluate for the presence of vasospasm. Vasospasm usually begins no earlier than 72 hours following the onset of bleeding, with a peak incidence on days 7-8. Similarly, this will also present with sudden deterioration in neurological status. All patients should receive nimodipine and euvolaemia should be maintained to reduce the risk of poor outcomes from vasospasm and ensuing delayed cerebral ischaemia.

A lumbar puncture has limited utility in evaluating for xanthochromia - from the breakdown of red blood cells in the cerebrospinal fluid - in patients with a delayed presentation of subarachnoid haemorrhage when the sensitivity of a CT Head is lower.

While an MRI head is a sensitive test for the evaluation of subarachnoid bleeds, there are often resource and duration limitations that can impede the timely assessment of a neurologically deteriorating patient.

Finally, an ECG may show 'cerebral t-waves' in the setting of a subarachnoid haemorrhage but is unlikely to explain the cause of this patient's GCS deterioration.

question:
A 62-year-old man comes into the emergency department due to increased double vision. He has been finding it increasingly difficult to walk down stairs because he is seeing two of every step. However, he is able to walk upstairs without any problems. The patient also reports trouble whilst reading the newspaper.

Upon further questioning he denies any recent eye trauma, headache or any weakness or numbness of his limbs. He suffers from hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, both of which are well controlled. The patient is a non-smoker and denies use of recreational drugs or alcohol.

Which of the following structures has most likely been affected?
explanation:
Vision worse going down stairs? Think 4th nerve palsy

This patient likely has trochlear nerve palsy (CN IV).  Microvascular disease can involved CN IV in older patients with cardiovascular risk factors. The trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle which causes the eye to internally rotate and depress while adducted.

Patients with trochlear nerve palsy usually present with vertical diplopia, most noticeable when the affected eye looks down and nasally. Clinical examination would show impairment of downgaze when the affected eye is adducted.

Abducens nerve (CN VI) innervates the lateral rectus which abducts they eye. A lesion affecting this nerve would cause horizontal diplopia and inward deviation of the eye.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) innervates; superior and inferior recti, medial rectus and inferior oblique muscles. Palsies to this nerve would present with impaired horizontal eye movement and weak adduction of the affected eye.

Loss of vision would result from damage to the optic nerve (CN II).

The trigeminal nerve does not supply motor function to the ocular muscles.

question:
A 16-year-old girl is seen in the clinic with suspected complex partial seizures following several episodes of impaired consciousness and automatic features including lip-smacking and chewing. Further investigation confirms the likely diagnosis, and the child is started on a medication for the condition.

A few days later however the child is rushed into hospital with a several, global rash with blistering and peeling of the skin. The mucous membranes are also involved and there is evidence of end-organ failure.

What medication was the child most likely started on?
explanation:
A rare but recognised adverse effect of lamotrigine therapy is Stevens-Johnson syndrome

This child has developed features clearly in keeping with the potential life-threatening skin reaction Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS). Although potential causes include viral infection and malignancies, drug reactions are by far the most common cause of SJS. Several medication can be responsible for SJS including two main anti-epileptics; phenytoin and

lamotrigine

. The other anti-epileptics options are not commonly known to be associated with the condition.

Levetiracetam

, commonly known by its brand name Keppra, is an anti-epileptic used in the management of partial-onset, myoclonic or tonic-clonic seizures. Compared to other anti-epileptics, the incidences of SJS with levetiracetam are extremely low with only sparse reporting of a potential association.

Sodium valproate

, another common anti-epileptic is rarely associated with SJS and in most reported incidences it is found that other drugs along with valproate were administered.  Severe side effects associated with sodium valproate include hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and fetal abnormalities in pregnancy.

Topiramate

is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor mainly used in the management of migraines, but it is also still used for both generalised and partial seizures. As a less commonly used anti-epileptic, topiramate is often used in complex seizures in children. It is also used in the management of overuse/rebound headaches secondary to chronic analgesia use. Topiramate is not associated with SJS, with side effects including impaired cognition, paraesthesia and rarely metabolic acidosis.

Valpromide

is a derivative of valproic acid also used for the treatment of epilepsy and some affective disorders. It has a similar side effect profile as sodium valproate and again is not associated with SJS.

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a two month history of electric shock like pains on the right side of her face. She describes having around 10-20 episodes a day which, each lasting for around 30-60 seconds. A recent dental check was normal. Neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most suitable first-line management?
explanation:
Trigeminal neuralgia - carbamazepine is first-line

The correct answer in this case is

Carbamazepine

. The patient's symptoms of electric shock-like pains on one side of her face, with multiple episodes a day lasting for 30-60 seconds, are highly suggestive of trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine is the first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia according to UK guidelines. It works by stabilizing the voltage-gated sodium channels in neurons, which helps to reduce the frequency and severity of the painful episodes.

Amitriptyline

is an incorrect choice because it is a tricyclic antidepressant that can be used as an adjuvant therapy in neuropathic pain but not as a primary treatment for trigeminal neuralgia. It may be considered if other first-line treatments are contraindicated or ineffective.

Sodium valproate

is also incorrect as it is primarily used as an antiepileptic medication and mood stabilizer. While it has some efficacy in treating neuropathic pain, it is not recommended as a first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

Atenolol

is a beta-blocker typically prescribed for hypertension and angina management; it has no role in the management of trigeminal neuralgia and therefore would not be appropriate in this scenario.

Finally,

Zolmitriptan

is incorrect because it is a triptan medication used specifically for the acute treatment of migraines and cluster headaches. It does not have any significant benefit in managing trigeminal neuralgia symptoms.

In summary, given the patient's presentation consistent with trigeminal neuralgia, Carbamazepine would be the most suitable first-line management option according to UK guidelines.

question:
A 29-year-old woman presents to her GP with fatigue. She says that for the last few months she has felt weak, particularly towards the end of the day. She does not report any change in sleeping habit, mood, diet or weight. She also says that she sometimes gets double vision.

On examination she has a partial ptosis bilaterally but more noticeable on the left, and the rest of her cranial nerves are normal. Her power is 4/5 all limbs, and her sensation and reflexes are intact.

What is the pathophysiology underlying the likely diagnosis?
options: Demyelination of the central nervous system
Demyelination of the peripheral nervous system
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis - antibodies against acetylcholine receptors

The history is suggestive of myasthenia gravis, which causes dysfunction at the neuromuscular junction due to the body forming antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor.

Neurological symptoms associated with cerebral infarction would usually be unilateral, with an abrupt onset and non-fluctuating course.

Demyelination of the central nervous system is the pathophysiology in multiple sclerosis (MS). This is an important differential to consider, but the history is more typical of myasthenia gravis. In particular, the typical eye symptom in MS is optic neuritis - painful loss of vision.

Demyelination of the peripheral nervous system is the pathophysiology in Guillain-Barre syndrome. In this condition you would expect the weakness to be progressive and reflexes to be diminished.

Inclusion bodies in motor neurones causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a type of motor neurone disease. In this condition you would expect the weakness to be progressive and associated with muscle stiffness/spasms. The extra-ocular muscles are usually spared until late in the disease, so the eye symptoms make this diagnosis less likely.

question:
A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden onset double vision on rightward gaze. He had a background of ischaemic heart disease and hypercholesterolemia. He smoked 10 cigarettes per day.

On examination, he was found to have a normal gait and a normal peripheral neurological examination. Examination of the cranial the left eye did not adduct on rightward gaze and the right eye exhibited nystagmus. The pupils were equal and reactive the light.

The emergency department team arrange an urgent MRI of the brain to rule out a possible stroke.

Where is the neurological lesion that would account for the clinical presentation?
explanation:
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is due to a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus

The patient here has presented with a typical history and examination of internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia occurs due to lesions in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which is located in the paramedian area of the midbrain and the pons. The patient has is at high risk for a stroke, with the previous past medical history and smoking history presented. Strokes can occur in the microvasculature of the midbrain, even with tiny areas of infarction, devastating consequences can arise.

In order to generate conjugate eye movements, a signal is sent from the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) to the pontine abducens nucleus. A signal is then sent from the abducens nucleus to the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle via the abducens nerve and to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus to control the contralateral medial rectus muscle. Fibres from the abducens nucleus cross the midline of the brainstem and form a highly myelinated tract, the MLF, which travels up the contralateral side of the brainstem to the oculomotor nucleus. The contralateral medial rectus muscle is then innervated from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain. The eye which fails to adduct is ipsilateral to the lesion in the MLF as the oculomotor nucleus does not receive a signal from the contralateral abducens nucleus to adduct. This results in a failure of conjugate gaze and diplopia.

The horizontal nystagmus of the right eye above is explained by Hering's law of equal innervation, whereby the 'weak, medial rectus muscle prompts the cortex to increase innervation to the oculomotor nucleus. This prompts an equally increased, and in this case, excessive innervation to the contralateral abducens nucleus, resulting in horizontal nystagmus of the right eye.

A lesion of the right abducens nucleus is incorrect. The right abducens nerve is functioning in the scenario above as the patient can look to the right and so we can assume that the nucleus is functioning also. The fact that the right eye exhibits nystagmus is related to Hering's law as mentioned above.

The left and right oculomotor nuclei are incorrect. The nuclei of the oculomotor nerve innervate ipsilaterally, emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncles. Hence a lesion of the left oculomotor nucleus would affect the left eye and lesion of the right oculomotor nucleus would affect the right eye. Lesions of the oculomotor nuclei would result in more profound ophthalmoplegias with the eye often resting in the 'down and out' position, due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique contraction.

question: Which of the following features is least likely to be found in a patient with tuberous sclerosis?
Which one of the following is least recognised as a cause of autonomic neuropathy

A 74-year-old man presents with sudden onset left arm weakness, dysphasia and a left-sided facial droop which started one hour ago.

He has a background of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolaemia. He lives with his wife and is usually independent of all activities of daily living, regularly playing golf with friends.

On examination, he has increased tone and 2/5 power throughout his left arm. His National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score is 9.

CT head shows an ischaemic lesion in the right hemisphere without evidence of haemorrhagic transformation. Magnetic resonance angiography confirms occlusion of the proximal anterior circulation.

What is the best next step in management?
explanation:
A combination of thrombolysis AND thrombectomy is recommend for patients with an acute ischaemic stroke who present within 4.5 hours

NICE updated their guidelines for stroke in 2019. One of the most recent developments has been the recommendation to offer thrombectomy, together with thrombolysis, for patients who have a confirmed occlusion of the proximal anterior circulation on imaging. NICE have also made recommendations to use a modified Rankin score of less than 3 and a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of more than 5 when considering the selection of patients for mechanical thrombectomy.

This patient has a good premorbid status and an NIHSS score of 9. He would thus meet the criteria for a combination of thrombolysis and thrombectomy. For patients presenting within 4.5 hours and not meeting these criteria, thrombolysis is still recommended - provided there are no contraindications and haemorrhagic stroke has been excluded on imaging.

Clopidogrel would be used for secondary prevention of stroke but not in the acute setting. If both aspirin and clopidogrel were contraindicated or not tolerated, dipyridamole could be used for this purpose.

Intravenous heparin has a number of uses, including the treatment of venous thrombosis and acute peripheral arterial occlusion. It is no longer used in the acute management of ischaemic stroke, however, as it is associated with an increased risk of cerebral and systemic bleeding.

question: A 44-year-old woman presents with a three month history of worsening involuntary movements of the head. These are worse when she is stressed and improved by alcohol. They are not present when she is sleep. There are no other neurological symptoms of note and neurological examination is unremarkable other than spotaneous movements of the head which are worse when she looks to either side. Her father had a similar complaint but never sought medical attention. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 42-year-old woman presents as she has noticed a 'droop' in the right side of her face since she woke up this morning. There is no associated limb weakness, dysphagia or visual disturbance. On examination you notice right-sided upper and lower facial paralysis. Which one of the following features would be most consistent with a diagnosis of Bell's palsy?
options: Sensory loss over the distribution of the facial nerve
Pins and needles in the right arm

question: A 70-year-old man is investigated for involuntary, jerking movements of his arms. His symptoms seem to resolve when he is asleep. Damage to which one of the following structures may lead to hemiballism?
explanation:
Hemiballism is caused by damage to the subthalamic nucleus

The correct answer is the

subthalamic nucleus

. Hemiballism is a rare syndrome characterised by involuntary, violent, flinging movements of the limbs on one side of the body. It is most commonly caused by damage to the subthalamic nucleus, a part of the basal ganglia that plays a crucial role in motor control. The subthalamic nucleus interacts with other structures in the basal ganglia to regulate movement. When it's damaged - often due to stroke or trauma - it can lead to disinhibition of thalamocortical output, resulting in uncontrolled movements typical of hemiballism.

The

substantia nigra

is more associated with Parkinson's disease than hemiballism. This structure produces dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement and coordination. Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons within the substantia nigra leads to decreased dopamine levels and results in Parkinson's disease, characterised by bradykinesia (slowness of movement), resting tremor, rigidity and postural instability.

Damage to the

red nucleus

doesn't typically result in hemiballism either. The red nucleus is involved in motor coordination but its exact role isn't fully understood. Lesions here may cause problems with coordinated movement or gait but not the characteristic flinging movements seen in hemiballism.

Similarly, lesions affecting the

globus pallidus

, another part of the basal ganglia, are not typically associated with hemiballism but rather with dystonia or parkinsonian symptoms. The globus pallidus works together with other structures within the basal ganglia to modulate voluntary movement.

Finally, damage to the

frontal lobe

can cause a variety of motor and cognitive symptoms given its involvement in many aspects of brain function including personality traits, decision-making and voluntary movement control. However, it's not typically implicated as a cause for hemiballism which is more closely related to specific structures within the basal ganglia such as subthalamic nucleus.

question: A 55-year-old man presents complaining of visual disturbance. Examination reveals a right congruous homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation:
Visual field defects:

The correct answer is the

Left occipital cortex

. A congruous homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing is indicative of a lesion in the occipital lobe, particularly in the primary visual cortex. The term 'congruous' refers to the mirror-image nature of the visual field defect in both eyes, which suggests that the lesion is located posterior to the optic tract. The term 'macula sparing' refers to the preservation of central vision, which is a characteristic feature of lesions in the occipital lobe due to dual blood supply from both middle and posterior cerebral arteries.

The

Right optic nerve

option would typically present as monocular vision loss rather than homonymous hemianopia. Damage at this level would affect only one eye because it occurs before the decussation (crossing) of optic nerve fibres at the chiasm.

Similarly, a lesion in the

Right optic radiation

would result in a left homonymous hemianopia. This is because right optic radiations carry information from left visual fields after decussation has occurred at the level of the optic chiasm.

A lesion in the

Left optic tract

would lead to a right homonymous hemianopia but it would be incongruous rather than congruous. Incongruity typically indicates a lesion anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus i.e., at the level of either optic tract or chiasm.

Finally, an injury at the level of

Optic chiasm

, such as caused by pituitary adenomas or craniopharyngiomas, usually leads to bitemporal hemianopia (loss of the outer/temporal half of visual field in both eyes). This occurs due to damage to crossing nasal fibres from each retina that carry temporal visual field information.

question:
A 19-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. An MRI brain is requested and it reveals what are likely to be bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

What neurocutaneous syndrome is the patient very likely to have?
explanation:
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas

Neurofibromatosis type 2 is a rare neurocutaneous syndrome. A classical feature includes bilateral vestibular schwannomas (previously known as acoustic neuromas), which present as a sensorineural hearing loss. Patients may have multiple schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas of the brain or spine. Other findings include retinal hamartomas, cataracts, Cafe Au Lait markings and peripheral nerve tumours.

Neurofibromatosis type 1, also known as von Recklinghausen disease, does not typically feature bilateral vestibular schwannomas. The typical features are Cafe au Lait spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas and optic nerve gliomas.

Von Hippel Lindau syndrome is a condition featuring visceral cysts and benign tumours in any system, including the brain. It is not associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

Tuberous sclerosis is a rare genetic disorder due to mutation of either the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Its features are multiple central nervous system hamartomas (tubers), subependymal giant cell astrocytomas of the brain, kidneys angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, facial angiofibromas, Shagreen patches and retinal astrocytic hamartomas.

Sturge Weber syndrome characterised by a 'port-wine stain' of the forehead, learning disabilities, seizures and glaucoma.

question:
An 18-year-old man presents for a general health review. He is currently well in himself, although has a complex past medical history involving recurrent chest infections and prominent difficulties with gait and movement since early childhood.

On examination, gait and limb coordination and movement difficulties are evident. Truncal instability is noted and tendon reflexes are absent. Distinct blood vessels are visible in both eyes, giving a 'bloodshot' appearance. Similar vessels are also prominent on the ear lobes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ataxic telangiectasia is characterised by cerebellar ataxia and telangiectasia, onset is in childhood

This patient's history, and examination findings, are highly suggestive of

ataxia telangiectasia

(AT). This is an autosomal recessive disorder that presents in early childhood, with onset typically around the age of 1 to 5 years. Patients experience significant ataxia due to cerebellar dysfunction, in addition to IgA deficiency - resulting in recurrent chest infections as seen here - as well as classic telangiectasias of the eyes and sun-exposed areas.

There is some overlap with

Friedrich's ataxia

(FA), in that it is also a cause of cerebellar ataxia and is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. However, its onset is typically around the age of 10 to 15 years. It has other features not present here, including optic atrophy, kyphoscoliosis and a link with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

Fragile-X tremor-ataxia syndrome

(FXTAS) is another cause of ataxia, although typically occurs in much older men and family history is more likely to be present. Tremor and autonomic deficits are more characteristic of FXTAS. Given the description of telangiectasias and young onset here, AT is more likely.

Niemann-Pick disease type C

(NP-C) presents with progressive neurodegeneration, developmental and speech delay, cataplexy and seizures, none of which are present here. Although gait ataxia is also present, the absence of the other features makes this less likely.

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)

disease is a rare genetic disorder involving multiple systems. Whilst also associated with cerebellar dysfunction and issues with balance and coordination, it is typically associated with retinal haemangioblastoma, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma, none of which are present here.

question:
A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe headache that started whilst at work 12 hours ago. He has no significant past medical history. He admits to being a frequent user of cocaine.

On examination, he appears to be in significant pain and distress. There are no signs of confusion. Neurological assessment is unremarkable. An urgent CT scan of the head is requested, which shows no acute abnormalities.

What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
explanation:
If subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected but a CT head done > 6 hours after symptom onset is normal, a lumbar puncture should be done to confirm or exclude the diagnosis

This patient's presentation of a sudden-onset severe headache is in keeping with subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). It is often described by patients as the worst headache that they have ever experienced. There is no history of trauma mentioned in this scenario and so this is likely to be a spontaneous SAH. It may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting, as well as signs of meningism - photophobia and neck stiffness. Non-contrast CT head is the initial investigation of choice. If done within 6 hours of onset and is normal, an alternative diagnosis should be considered. However, if done more than 6 hours after onset, as is the case here, a

lumbar puncture

should urgently be performed to assess for xanthochromia and raised opening pressure. If confirmed SAH, an immediate referral to neurosurgery is warranted.

A

CT angiogram of the head

may be used in the context of SAH. However, it is used after spontaneous SAH is confirmed, rather than diagnostically, to identify the underlying cause - for instance, an aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation.

MRI scanning of the head

is not routinely used in the investigation of SAH, as CT head is sufficient. If the CT head is normal, a lumbar puncture should be performed next.

Temporal artery biopsy

is used to assess for evidence of giant cell arteritis (GCA). Although also presenting with a headache, this typically presents with temporal tenderness, jaw claudication and often a background of polymyalgia rheumatica. This does not fit with the scenario here, which is more likely to be SAH.

A

urine drug screen

may be useful to rule out cocaine as the underlying cause of the headache. However, it does not change the fact that a lumbar puncture is the most important step to definitively exclude SAH.

question:
A 44-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of weakness in his hands and legs and numbness in his feet. He first noticed some problems with walking in his late teens and reports that he's always been 'clumsy' and will often trip over. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medications. On examination, he has a high-stepping gait with wasting of the lower legs and high arches. Power is reduced in all limbs and reflexes are difficult to elicit. There is a reduction in sensation which is more pronounced distally. Coordination is intact.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease can affect both motor and sensory peripheral nerves

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy. UMN signs are not present in these patients. Patients can present with lower motor neurone signs in all limbs and reduced sensation (more pronounced distally).

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an inherited myopathy. It is caused by progressive degeneration and weakness of specific muscle groups. Most patients lose the ability to walk by 12 years of age and require ventilatory support by the age of 25. Sensation is intact in these patients.

Cervical spondylosis is the term used for osteoarthritis of the spine and can result in compression of the spinal cord. This is more likely to result in LMN signs at the level of the compression (ie. upper limb if the lesion is below C5) with UMN signs below (in the lower limb). Patients usually complain of neck pain and stiffness.

Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an inflammatory peripheral sensory and motor neuropathy. It typically presents over the course of days to weeks, not years. There is often a recent bacterial or viral infection in the history.

Patients with subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SCDC) classically have an ataxic gait (due to degeneration of the dorsal columns) and mixed UMN and LMN signs (due to degeneration of lateral motor tracts and peripheral nerves). The history will typically be subacute, occurring over months rather than decades. Patients with SCDC often notice sensory symptoms before weakness.

question:
A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a one-hour history of right-sided weakness and facial droop, which has now entirely resolved. He has a past medical history of migraines with aura, which started around 8 years ago, and low mood. He had a similarly brief episode of sudden dizziness and slurred speech six months ago but did not seek medical attention. His father had similar experiences in his 50s but died in a road traffic accident aged 60.

The patient's CT head is normal. He has an MRI head which shows a number of hyperintense lesions. What is the most likely cause for his symptoms?
explanation:
CADASIL is a rare cause of multiple cerebral infarctions

The correct answer is CADASIL - cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. This is a genetic condition due to a mutation in the NOCTH3 gene. It usually presents with the onset of migraines in middle age, followed by recurrent TIAs and strokes, and resulting in neuro-cognitive decline, psychiatric problems and dementia. MRI often shows multiple widespread hyper-intense lesions in the white matter, basal ganglia, thalamus and pons.

CADASIL foundation:

https://www.cadasilfoundation.org/what.html

question:
A 55-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with reports of recurrent episodes of the room spinning. He has no past medical history. He denies hearing loss or aural fullness. The patient experiences this commonly when he is in bed and each episode lasts 10-20 seconds. This has been ongoing for months and was preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection. He is well in between episodes.

The examination is unremarkable.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Typical BPPV history:

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

is correct. The patient gives a clear history short lasting stereotyped episodes of vertigo. Given this is commonly occurring when he is in bed it suggests that rolling over in bed is contributory, which would be typical of this diagnosis (brought about by changes in head position).

Meniere's disease

is incorrect. This can cause recurrent episodes of vertigo. However, it will be unrelated to head position, episodes typically last 2-3 hours and there may be other associated features like hearing loss and a sensation of aural fullness.

Multiple sclerosis

is incorrect. Vertigo is uncommon in MS. If it occurs, it is unlikely to be short-lasting. Additionally, there would typically be other associated features e.g. clinical signs of an upper motor neuron disorder or optic neuritis. It would be unrelated to the position a patient takes.

Posterior circulation stroke

is incorrect. If the patient had a stroke it would be a sudden onset of persistent vertigo rather than recurrent episodes with periods of being well in between. The examination may be abnormal.

Viral labyrinthitis

is incorrect. This can cause vertigo. However, it would typically cause vertigo after an infection that would result in one continuous episode that subsequently resolves rather than recurrent episodes. In this case, the infection that preceded the symptoms is unrelated. Furthermore, viral labyrinthitis causes

hearing loss

(unlike vestibular neuritis), which is absent here and makes the diagnosis unlikely.

question: A 60-year-old woman presents with a tremor. Which one of the following features would suggest a diagnosis of essential tremor rather than Parkinson's disease?
options: Tremor is worse when the arms are outstretched
correctText: Tremor is worse when the arms are outstretched

question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of blurred vision in her right eye and pain with eye movement. One year prior, she experienced sudden weakness and stiffness in her left leg, which resolved over three days. She also reports a transient decrease in colour perception six months ago. Examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect and optic disc swelling on the right side.

Which MRI sequence is most appropriate for identifying the characteristic lesions associated with this condition?
explanation:
Use MRI FLAIR sequence in diagnosis of multiple sclerosis vs. MRI STIR in flares of thyroid eye disease

The

MRI FLAIR sequence

is the correct answer. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is defined by recurrent neurological symptoms. The patient presents with blurred vision in her right eye, associated with pain on movement, and has experienced weakness and stiffness in the limbs that resolved over three days a year previously, as well as a transient reduction in colour perception six months ago. These clinical features are indicative of MS and align with its relapsing-remitting nature, where patients undergo exacerbations followed by periods of remission. MRI FLAIR sequences are particularly adept at identifying hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted images, which are characteristic of MS; they effectively reveal lesions within periventricular areas and can detect the pathognomonic Dawson fingers that extend perpendicular to the corpus callosum. This imaging modality is proficient at detecting disseminated lesions across both time and space, which are crucial criteria for diagnosing MS.

The

MRI diffusion-weighted sequence

is primarily utilised for detecting acute ischaemic strokes by highlighting areas of restricted diffusion. However, it is not the optimal choice for visualising chronic lesions typical of MS since it focuses on changes in water molecule diffusion within brain tissue – a feature not commonly associated with MS lesions.

The

MRI STIR sequence

is widely used in soft tissue imaging and is particularly useful for detecting oedema and inflammation in various conditions. It plays a significant role in evaluating thyroid eye disease due to its sensitivity to oedema and ability to assess soft tissue involvement. Nevertheless, other MRI sequences offer superior visualisation of demyelinating plaques found in MS.

The

MRI susceptibility-weighted sequence

is invaluable for identifying microhaemorrhages or iron deposits within cerebral tissues in conditions such as haemochromatosis. It also has applications in cases involving cerebral microhaemorrhages and vascular anomalies but falls short in depicting key features of MS like periventricular plaques and Dawson fingers.

The

MRI T1-weighted sequence

provides high-resolution images that delineate anatomical structures clearly and can be essential when assessing brain anatomy and atrophy. However, it has limited sensitivity for high-signal lesions prevalent in MS; these lesions are more conspicuously identified on T2-weighted or FLAIR sequences. Although T1-weighted sequences can show contrast-enhancing lesions signifying active inflammation, they are less sensitive when it comes to detecting chronic non-enhancing lesions.

question:
A 35-year-old man is brought into the emergency department after being assaulted and robbed 1 hour ago. He states he was struck on his head and upper body with a crowbar before being knocked unconscious. He has nausea, right-sided headache, and severe right forearm pain with deformity but denies chest and abdominal pain. He has a history of diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia.

His blood pressure is 168/88 mmHg, heart rate 55 beats/min and respiratory rate 14 breaths/min. During the examination, the patient becomes obtunded.

What finding is most likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Petechial rash overlying anterior chest wall
explanation:
Raised ICP can cause a third nerve palsy due to herniation

This patient likely has an epidural haematoma that has caused transtentorial herniation. This is evidenced by the history of head trauma, a lucid interval, signs of increased intracranial pressure and a resultant decrease in consciousness resulting in obtundation. Increased pressure within the cranium secondary to the rapid expansion of intracranial haematoma can cause the temporal lobe to herniate through the tentorial notch. This herniation can compress the ipsilateral third cranial nerve, resulting in a

dilated pupil

, ptosis and 'down and out' eye deviation.

Increased JVP
