question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension and epilepsy is noted to have gingival hyperplasia on examination in the cardiology clinic. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Gingival hyperplasia: phenytoin, ciclosporin, calcium channel blockers and AML

The correct answer is

Nifedipine

. Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker used in the treatment of hypertension. One of its well-documented side effects is gingival hyperplasia, which occurs due to an overgrowth of the gum tissue. The exact mechanism of this side effect is not fully understood but it's suggested that nifedipine may alter collagen metabolism, thereby leading to an accumulation of extracellular matrix and resultant gingival overgrowth.

Sodium valproate

is an antiepileptic drug used for the management of seizures. Its common side effects include gastrointestinal disturbances, tremor, weight gain and hair loss. Gingival hyperplasia is not typically associated with sodium valproate use.

Lisinopril

is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor used in the management of hypertension and heart failure. Common side effects are cough, dizziness, rash and renal impairment. It does not commonly cause gingival hyperplasia.

Atorvastatin

belongs to the statin group of drugs and is primarily used for lowering cholesterol levels in patients at high risk of cardiovascular disease. While it can cause various side effects such as myalgia, hepatic impairment or even rhabdomyolysis in severe cases, gingival hyperplasia isn't a known complication associated with atorvastatin use.

Finally,

Carbamazepine

, another antiepileptic drug like sodium valproate, has several potential adverse effects including dizziness, ataxia and blood dyscrasias but it doesn't typically result in gingival hyperplasia either.

question: Which one of the following is least associated with the development of chorea?

A 23-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department following a stabbing incident. He has multiple lacerations to his flank and lower back which have been caused by a knife. After being stabilized he complains of his right leg 'feeling funny.'

You perform a full neurological examination which reveals the following:

weakness in extension and flexion of the right knee
loss of proprioception and vibration below mid thigh in the right leg
loss of pain sensation below the mid thigh in left leg

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following best describes the trauma?
options: Hemisection of anterior section of spinal cord
Right-sided lateral hemisection of spinal cord
Left-sided lateral hemisection of spinal cord
correctText: Right-sided lateral hemisection of spinal cord
explanation:
Brown-Sequard syndrome is a result of lateral hemisection of the spinal cord

The patient has Brown-Sequard syndrome, which is a lateral hemisection of spinal cord. It causes same sided weakness and proprioception/vibration loss and loss of pain/temperature on the opposite side to the hemisection. This is because the pathway for pain/temperature sensation decussates at the level of the nerve root.

Damage to the sciatic nerve would produce unilateral symptoms. Anterior hemisection is rare and unlikely given the mechanism of injury. It would also produce a different distribution of neurological symptoms. A left-sided hemisection would cause ipsilateral weakness. A posterior disk prolapse is also unlikely given the mechanism of trauma.

question:
A 55-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with sensory loss.

On examination he has loss of fine touch, joint position sense and temperature sensation bilaterally in the lower limbs, extending from his knees down, as well as in his fingertips.

His motor function is 5/5 in all four limbs.

His medications include: calcichew, alfacalcidol, sodium bicarbonate and ramipril

Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of these clinical findings?
explanation:
Uraemic polyneuropathy is predominantly sensory

Of the above, CKD (leading to uraemia) is the only option to cause a predominantly sensory polyneuropathy.

Guillain-Barre syndrome and lead poisoning cause a polyneuropathy which is predominantly motor.

Polio and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis affect the anterior horn cells of the motor tract, within the spinal cord. As such, they cause a motor deficit.

question:
An 83-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with reduced consciousness. His daughter reports that he has been behaving out of character over the past three weeks, with aggressive outbursts followed by excessive sleepiness. The daughter also describes an episode of increased confusion 3 days ago which resolved after 24 hours. This morning the patient was found unresponsive in bed. His past medical history includes atrial fibrillation and recurrent falls. On examination, he is responding only to pain. There is no obvious focal neurology.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fluctuating consciousness = subdural haemorrhage

The correct answer is

subdural haemorrhage.

This patient's presentation of fluctuating confusion and reduced consciousness, is highly suggestive of a chronic subdural haematoma. Recurrent falls and increased age are further risk factors which support this diagnosis, as well as the possibility that he is taking anticoagulation for his atrial fibrillation.

Extradural haematoma

is incorrect. Extradural haematomas typically cause symptoms quickly after injury due to their arterial origin and high-pressure bleeding. This does not fit with the clinical presentation here.

Ischaemic stroke

is incorrect. This would more typically present with focal neurology and acute onset of symptoms, neither of which are described in this patient.

Space-occupying lesion

is incorrect. Although this could present with confusion and reduced consciousness, the history of recurrent falls and fluctuating confusion make subdural haemorrhage the most likely diagnosis in this case.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage

is incorrect. This typically presents with a sudden onset, 'thunderclap' headache, rather than the prolonged disturbance in consciousness that is described here. Additionally, subarachnoid haemorrhage has different associated risk factors of arterio-venous malformations, polycystic kidney disease and hypertension.

question: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Which one of the following drugs has been shown to confer a survival benefit?
explanation:
Motor neuron disease - riluzole

The correct answer is

Riluzole

. Riluzole is a glutamate antagonist which has been shown to slow the progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and confer a survival benefit. The NICE guideline NG42 recommends offering riluzole to people with ALS to slow disease progression. It works by decreasing the release of glutamate, thereby reducing neuronal excitotoxicity, which is thought to play a role in the pathogenesis of ALS.

Rituximab

is an incorrect option. Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody used primarily in the treatment of B-cell malignancies such as non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. It can also be used in some autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis, but there is no evidence that it confers any benefit in ALS.

Interferon-beta

is another incorrect choice. Interferon-beta is primarily used in the management of multiple sclerosis (MS), not ALS. It helps reduce inflammation and prevent nerve damage in MS but does not have any proven benefit in slowing down or halting the progression of ALS.

Moving on to

Cyclophosphamide

, this drug is also not used for treating ALS. Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating chemotherapeutic agent, employed mainly for treating various types of cancer including lymphomas, leukaemias, and some solid tumours. It works by interfering with DNA replication, thus inhibiting cell division.

Finally,

Interferon-alpha

does not confer a survival benefit in patients with ALS either. Similar to interferon-beta, interferon-alpha has antiviral properties and can modulate immune responses. It's used predominantly for treating hepatitis C and certain haematological malignancies like hairy cell leukaemia but not for neurodegenerative diseases like ALS.

question: A 64-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with increased difficulty in walking. On examination there is weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and of the extensor hallucis longus associated with loss of sensation on the lateral aspect of the lower leg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common peroneal nerve lesion can cause weakness of foot dorsiflexion and foot eversion

The most likely diagnosis in this case is

common peroneal nerve palsy

. The common peroneal nerve, also known as the common fibular nerve, is a branch of the sciatic nerve that supplies the muscles responsible for ankle dorsiflexion and extension of the toes, specifically the extensor hallucis longus. Damage to this nerve can result in foot drop and sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the lower leg, which are both symptoms described in this scenario.

Tibial nerve palsy

is an incorrect answer because it primarily affects the plantar flexors of the ankle and flexors of the toes. Sensory loss would be expected on the sole of the foot rather than on the lateral aspect of the lower leg.

Obturator nerve palsy

is another incorrect answer. The obturator nerve supplies muscles in the medial compartment of the thigh, which are responsible for hip adduction. A lesion affecting this nerve would not cause weakness in ankle dorsiflexion or sensory changes in the lower leg.

Lateral cutaneous nerve palsy

, also known as lateral femoral cutaneous nerve palsy or meralgia paraesthetica, is an incorrect answer because it only affects sensation over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh without any motor deficits. It does not cause weakness in ankle dorsiflexion or affect sensation on the lateral aspect of the lower leg.

Finally,

pudendal nerve palsy

is incorrect as well since it mainly affects muscles and sensation in genitalia and perineum area. It does not have any impact on muscles or sensations related to walking or movement of legs.

question: You are reviewing a 22-year-old man who has developed headaches. Which one of the following features is most typical of migraines?

A 67-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with his wife. She explains that, for several days, he has had difficulty talking. His speech is often broken and halting. She feels that he is understanding whatever is said to him. His past medical history includes hypertension and ischaemic heart disease.

On examination, he is unable to verbalise clearly - his speech is non-fluent and halting, managing 3 or 4 words at a time. He is unable to repeat phrases when asked. However, he is able to follow commands.

Which area of the brain is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
Broca's dysphasia: speech non-fluent, comprehension normal, repetition impaired

There are a number of types of aphasia, caused by different areas of the brain being affected and resulting in different signs and symptoms. This patient has Broca's (expressive) aphasia - characterised by non-fluent, laboured, halting speech. Repetition is impaired, but comprehension is normal. It is due to a lesion of the

inferior frontal gyrus

.

Conduction aphasia is classically due to a lesion of the

arcuate fasciculus

, which connects Wernicke's and Broca's areas. With these patients, speech is instead fluent, but repetition remains poor. They are typically aware of their errors.

The

precentral gyrus

is found on the surface of the posterior frontal lobe. It is the site of the primary motor cortex. It is not associated with Broca's aphasia.

Lesions of the

superior temporal gyrus

result in Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia. It presents with impaired comprehension and sentences that do not make sense - speech remains fluent but word substitution and neologisms result in a 'word salad'.

The

ventromedial prefrontal cortex

is found in the frontal lobe. It is involved in the processing of risk and fear, and inhibition of emotional responses. It is not associated with Broca's aphasia.

question:
A 74-year-old male patient is brought in to hospital by ambulance with right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. His wife reports that he was well the previous night and awoke with these symptoms one hour ago.

On initial assessment, he is noted to have an expressive aphasia, right-sided facial droop, and right-sided weakness most prominent in the upper extremity.

A non-contrast CT head does not reveal any intracranial haemorrhage. A CT angiogram reveals a clot in the first branch (M1) of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA). The patient does not have a history of previous intracranial haemorrhage, intracranial neoplasm, prior stroke or traumatic brain injury, or recent bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract.

Which of the following interventions is most likely to be of benefit in this patient?
explanation:
Large artery acute ischaemic stroke? Consider mechanical clot retrieval

The vignette describes a patient presenting with a left-sided large artery acute ischaemic stroke. The 'wake-up' nature of this stroke makes it difficult to ascertain the time of onset of symptoms. Whereas thrombolysis is contraindicated in this context, mechanical clot retrieval can be performed in patients with wake-up strokes who have a confirmed occlusion of the proximal anterior circulation (anterior cerebral artery or middle cerebral artery) demonstrated by computed tomography angiography or magnetic resonance angiography.

The window of thrombolysis in ischaemic strokes is 4.5 hours, beyond which the risk of haemorrhagic transformation outweighs the benefit. Other contraindications to thrombolysis include the presence of an intracranial neoplasm and recent major bleeding e.g. from the gastrointestinal tract. In patients with large vessel occlusions (LVO) presenting within 4.5 hours, there is no evidence to support better outcomes when combining mechanical thrombectomy with thrombolysis.

Treatment-dose anticoagulation has a role in the treatment of venous thromboembolic events in haemodynamically stable patients, but a limited role in the management of arterial ischaemic strokes. Of note, intravenous heparin therapy is given peri-procedurally during endovascular interventions such as mechanical thrombectomies.

Dual antiplatelet therapy is unlikely to reverse the ischaemic stroke in this patient. It does have a role in reducing the risk of in-stent thromboses following intracranial stenting and percutaneous coronary interventions, as well as some benefit in reducing the risk of cerebrovascular events in patients with intracranial stenoses.

question:
An 80-year-old man presents with sudden-onset difficulty walking and a droopy eyelid. He noticed slurred speech a few weeks ago, but as this resolved after 10 minutes he did not seek medical attention.

On general examination, he has an ataxic gait and loss of sensation in his right arm and leg. On examination of his cranial nerves, he has nystagmus to the left, ptosis, meiosis and loss of sensation on the left-hand side of the face.

Where is the likely arterial lesion?
explanation:
Lateral medullary syndrome - PICA lesion - cerebellar signs,  contralateral sensory loss & ipsilateral Horner's

Posterior inferior cerebellar

artery (PICA) is the correct answer. Left-sided Horner's syndrome depicted here with cerebellar signs and a contralateral sensory loss of the limbs is consistent with a left-sided PICA infarct. The lateral brainstem signs involve the sympathetic outflow tract, (hence Horner's with ptosis and meiosis), spinocerebellar tract (hence cerebellar signs), the sensory nucleus of cranial nerve V (hence the sensation over the left-hand side of the face would be affected) and spinothalamic tract (hence pain and temperature loss on the contralateral, right side in this case).

Anterior inferior cerebellar

artery (AICA) is incorrect as this does not affect the same region as the PICA and hence produces a different neurological deficit. The AICA lesions are less well known and have been purported to cause central vestibular loss and hearing loss, since the inner ear, lateral pons and anterior inferior cerebellum are supplied.

Pontine

is incorrect because this artery causes a variety of syndromes, with none of the syndromes creating the lateral medullary syndrome associated with PICA infarct. Pontine infarcts can cause the locked-in syndrome, pure motor hemiparesis, sensorimotor deficits, ataxic hemiparesis and more rarely dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome.

Posterior cerebral

is an incorrect answer. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe therefore an infarct here would cause a visual field loss or homonymous hemianopia to the contralateral side.

Superior cerebellar

is an incorrect answer as infarction in the superior cerebellar artery does not cause the brainstem signs seen in this case of PICA infarction. Superior cerebellar artery stroke commonly results in vertigo, dizziness, nystagmus, ataxias and sometimes mild hemiparesis.

question:
A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of two weeks of tingling in his feet and difficulty walking. He has no medical history. He frequently inhales nitrous oxide with his friends. His diet is normal.

On examination, there is impaired proprioception and vibration sense extending to the ankles. The plantar responses are extensor. The ankle reflexes are absent and the knee reflexes are brisk.

Blood tests:


Vitamin B12 level	700pg/ml	(200-900)

What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
correctText: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
explanation:
Distal sensory loss, tingling + absent ankle jerks/extensor plantars + gait abnormalities/Romberg's positive → subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

is correct. The patient uses nitrous oxide on a regular basis. This can cause a functional B12 deficiency (the B12 levels will be normal) and can give rise to subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord like in true B12 deficiency. In this setting, it is important to check a methylmalonic acid (MMA) level. In the setting of functional B12 deficiency, this will be high. This is characterized by dorsal column abnormalities (impaired vibration and proprioception sense), absent ankle jerks, extensor plantar responses, and brisk knee reflexes.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

is incorrect. This tends to cause a pure motor weakness with a combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs. Dorsal column involvement is not typical.

Guillain-Barre syndrome

is incorrect. This cause a lower motor neuron distribution of weakness +/- sensory loss. Extensor plantar responses are not a feature and therefore this is unlikely.

Pellagra

is incorrect. This is caused by niacin deficiency, which causes the syndrome of pellagra characterized by dementia and dermatitis and diarrhea, and ultimately, death. You may get extensor plantar responses and absent ankle jerks in this condition. However, it is very unlikely to develop in someone described as having a 'normal' diet. It is more likely to occur in food-limited populations.

Syphilis infection

is incorrect. This is a cause of absent ankle jerks and extensor plantar responses. However, there is no history of exposure and we are told he has a common reason to have a functional B12 deficiency and therefore this is a less likely diagnosis in this context.

question:
A 24-year-old man presents with lower limb weakness. He states that he had an episode of food poisoning two weeks ago which consisted of severe abdominal pain and profuse non-bloody diarrhoea. Following this, he noticed progressive difficulties with balance.

His past medical history is largely unremarkable, but he admits to intravenous drug use with heroin. He last injected heroin three weeks ago.

On examination, marked ataxia and ophthalmoplegia are noted.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Miller Fisher syndrome - areflexia, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia

Miller-Fisher syndrome

is correct. This subtype of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is characterised by areflexia, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Descending weakness is also a classic feature of this condition, as opposed to the ascending weakness seen in more common forms of GBS.

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy

is incorrect. This is the most common form of GBS, characterised by a rapidly evolving ascending weakness, mild sensory loss, and hypo- or areflexia. The presence of ataxia and ophthalmoplegia instead supports a diagnosis of Miller-Fisher syndrome.

Acute motor axonal neuropathy

is incorrect. This is a less common subtype of Guillain-Barre syndrome that presents with motor involvement only. There is often early and severe respiratory involvement. This is a less likely diagnosis here, given the presence of ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.

Botulism

is incorrect. Botulism is characterised by a descending, flaccid paralysis. It is important to note that the patient is an intravenous drug user which is a risk factor for botulism. However, this method of transmission would not explain the history of gastroenteritis features. These can, of course, be related to food-borne botulism. Regardless, the clinical features of ataxia and ophthalmoplegia are more in keeping with Miller-Fisher syndrome.

Tetanus

is incorrect. Tetanus is a life-threatening disease characterised by descending spastic paralysis. Although the causative bacteria

Clostridium tetani

has been found in contaminated heroin, the clinical features here are more suggestive of Miller-Fisher syndrome.

question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department. He was hit on the side the head by a cricket ball during a match. His teacher describes him initially collapsing to the ground and complaining of a sore head. After two minutes he got up, said he felt OK and continued playing. After 30 minutes he suddenly collapsed to the ground and lost consciousness. What type of injury is he most likely to have sustained?
explanation:
Head injury, lucid interval - extradural (epidural) haematoma

The most likely injury sustained by the 12-year-old boy in this scenario is an

extradural haematoma

. This type of injury typically occurs when there is a traumatic impact to the side of the head, which can cause a tear in the middle meningeal artery. The initial symptoms may be mild or transient, but as the bleeding continues and blood accumulates between the dura mater and skull, it can lead to rapid neurological deterioration due to increased intracranial pressure. The classic presentation of a 'lucid interval' followed by sudden collapse and loss of consciousness described in this case strongly suggests an extradural haematoma.

A

cerebral contusion

is less likely in this case, as it involves bruising of brain tissue due to direct trauma. While it is possible that the patient has some degree of cerebral contusion from being hit by a cricket ball, this would not typically result in the sudden collapse and loss of consciousness observed after a lucid interval.

A

subarachnoid haemorrhage

is also unlikely given the mechanism of injury and clinical presentation. Subarachnoid haemorrhages are usually caused by rupture of an intracranial aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation rather than blunt trauma. The sudden onset of severe headache (often described as 'thunderclap headache') would be more characteristic for subarachnoid haemorrhage, which was not reported in this case.

An

intraventricular haemorrhage

refers to bleeding within the ventricular system, often secondary to another type of intracranial bleed such as subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage. In this case, there is no indication that such bleeding has occurred based on history alone.

Finally, a

subdural haematoma

is a collection of blood between the dura mater and arachnoid membrane, usually caused by tearing of bridging veins due to acceleration-deceleration forces during trauma. While it could potentially occur in this scenario, the rapid neurological deterioration after a lucid interval is more suggestive of an extradural haematoma. Subdural haematomas typically present with a more gradual decline in consciousness over hours to days or even weeks.

question:
A 67-year-old man presents to his GP with numbness in his feet and recurrent falls over the past month. He describes difficulty walking. His GP recently started him on folate for a macrocytic anaemia. He takes no other regular medications. He does not drink alcohol. On examination, he has an ataxic gait and Romberg's test is positive. Examination of his lower limbs demonstrates an increase in tone and bilateral weakness. He has absent ankle and knee jerks with upgoing plantars. Light touch and vibration sense is reduced bilaterally.

What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
correctText: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
Always replace vitamin B12 before folate - giving folate to a patient deficient in B12 can precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the cord

Subacute combined degeneration of the cord involves degeneration of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord, often due to vitamin B12 deficiency.

Damage to the posterior columns - loss of proprioception, light touch and vibration sense (sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg's test).
Damage to lateral columns - spastic weakness and upgoing plantars (UMN signs).
Damage to peripheral nerves - absent ankle and knee jerks (LMN signs).

When there is a mix of UMN and LMN signs in a patient, always consider SCDC.

Replacing folate without vitamin B12 (hinted at in this case) can precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the cord in a patient who is vitamin B12 deficient.

Always ensure vitamin B12 levels are checked (and replenished) before giving folate for a macrocytic anaemia.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a subtype of motor neurone disease. This may present with mixed UMN and LMN signs but no associated sensory deficits.

Guillain-Barre syndrome is an inflammatory

peripheral

neuropathy so will not present with UMN signs. There is nothing in the history to suggest a recent bacterial or viral infection.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease affecting the

neuromuscular junction

so will not present with UMN signs or sensory loss.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary sensory and motor

peripheral

neuropathy. UMN signs are not present in these patients. However, patients can present with LMN signs in all limbs and reduced sensation (more pronounced distally).
